Mr. H. H. STEVENS (Vancouver) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 227, to amend, the Immigration Act. He said:
The House and the country are well aware of the difficulties which we have been encountering for a number of years past in dealing with immigration from the continent of Asia. At the present time we have three methods of dealing with this question. Japanese immigration is controlled by an amicable arrangement between the two governments; 'Chinese immigration is subject to a head tax of $500, and Hindu immigration comes under an Order in Council which provides that immigrants can only come by direct route to this country. This provision has for some time more or less effectively stopped this immigration. However, there has /been a great real of dissatisfaction. It has been recognized that the regulations now in force are more or less of a temporary character, and there is a general demand 
throughout the country, especially in the province from which I come, that the Dominion Government shall take some definite and final action towards the regulation and restriction of Asiatic immigration. The objections to exclusive regulations are based largely upon the desire of this Government, and the people of Canada as a whole, not to do anything which might offend the dignity of other peoples by specifying exclusion. In this sentiment I heartily concur, but it appears to me, and I think the events of recent years, especially those of the last month or so, have amply demonstrated that this is a case where we have to choose between two evils. One is the possibility of causing some slight offence to these people from across the seas, and the other is unrestricted Asiatic immigration into this country. We cannot go on with the temporary expedients which have been in force for the last few years. There are other reasons why more stringent immigration regulations have not, up to this time, been adopted. For instance, there is the imperial reason, and it is one which is of very great importance, but in that regard I would like to point out a principle which I think we should hold more dearly than any other principle of government, and that is that we, the people of the Dominion, or the people of any of the overseas dominions, or, to to control immigration into this country, have a right to control the immigration into their own country. I base my proposal on the principle that it is our right to control immigration into this country. We axe not bound to extend the privileges of our country to every one who cares to come. It is not a right on the part of immigrants to enter this country, but it is our right to restrict *whatever immigration we desire. For this position I have a very high authority. Lord Curzon, in discussing the Hindu immigration problem, has declared that:
The common rights of British citizenship cannot be held to override the rights of self-protection conferred on a self-governing colony.
That is exactly where I stand. I urge upon Parliament and upon the Government to take a firm stand upon that principle. Now-
Order.

speechtext:
Order; I am afraid that the hon. member is rather going beyond what is permissible, that is, merely to explain the principle of the Bill.

utr.17

I am simply offering this explanation to the House, as a reason for the introduction of this Bill. The Bill provides for an amendment to section 3 of the Immigration Act, which is the clause under which we exclude certain classes of people, for instance, the physically unfit, etc. I purpose by this Bill to add a clause to section 3 of the Immigration Act, which will exclude all natives and naturalized citizens of countries in Asia, south of the 50th parallel of north latitude, provided, however, that this clause shall not apply to any country the government of which has a specific arrangement with the Government of Canada. In other words, we fix the principle of excluding immigrants from Asia, but if the Government of a country in Asia wishes to enter into an arrangement with our Government in order to protect their national dignity, we leave the door open for them to do so.
I urge this Bill upon the attention of the Government, and if possible I should like to see it passed this session. Possibly there may have to be representations made to the Home authorities with respect to it, and if it should be found consequently impossible to pass it this session, then I urge upon the Government that they should make strong recommendations to the Home authorities, with regard to this very important matter, so that this Bill may pass at the next session.

My hon. friend has introduced this Bill when, as everybody knows, we are so near prorogation that it is expected we shall be able to finish all the business before us within the present week. The hon. gentleman is aware that, even if we had a month or six weeks still remaining of the session, it would be impossible to press this Bill through. The Bill, of course, cannot be taken up at all without the consent of the Government, and it would be interesting to know whether the Government intends to adopt this Bill and to support its passage.

Sir,-The mail service between Canada and Great Britain is a disgrace to both governments. I am ready to endorse this statement, which is quoted from a letter to Mr. C. N. Armstrong in the Times of May 13.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is hardly permissible for the hon. member to occupy the time of the House with reading what he calls a circular letter; but on account of the urgency of the situation, the matter might reasonably be allowed to pass. It is, however, rather an abuse of the privileges of the House.

I recognize your point, Sir. It is a very urgent matter, and I just wish to call the attention of the Government to it. This circular letter, in conjunction with a resolution passed by the municipal council of Winnipeg calling upon the Government to stop immigration until labour conditions improve, would show that these conditions were not confined to eastern Canada, but were prevalent in western Canada as well. Is it the intention of the Government to appoint a Royal Commission, as requested by the Montreal Trades and Labour Council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The circular letter or
memorial to which the hon. gentleman

alludes has not yet reached me. It was apparently posted on Saturday, and therefore I suppose in the ordinary course I should receive it to-day; but up to, the present it has not come to hand. It is possible that persons out of employment may have been attracted to Montreal in very large numbers owing to the hopes that were held out of immediate employment being offered there to all persons who should desire it; but I do not know about that. As far as immigration is concerned on the Pacific coast and along the international boundary through the United States into British Columbia, the immigration of labourers and artisans has already been prohibited since the 1st of January last. As far as the eastern seaboard is concerned, the Department of Immigration has already sent out notices on two different occasions during the last two or three months emphasizing the instructions that the immigration of labourers and artisans is not desirable; and that the only persons whose immigration would be desirable in Canada at the present time are agricultural settlers and labourers and female domestic servants. I am not sure of the exact tenor of the notice which has been sent out, but it is very much in the same terms as the two notices which were sent out under similar circumstances by the late Administration in the winter and spring of 1908. AVe have observed the same precautions with regard to this particular matter, and had in mind conditions of a very similar character. As far as the appointment of a Royal Commission is concerned, I cannot, of course, make any announcement, as the subject has not yet been under the consideration of the Government, for the reason that I have not yet received the memorial.

(Minister of Trade
and Commerce):	We have had for
many years a service from the western portion of Canada to China and Japan, under contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway and Steamship Company. That service has been a composite one in so far as its support is concerned; that is, the British Government has co-operated with the Canadian Government. That contract came to a conclusion a little more than a year ago, and a contention arose between the British post office and our post office as to the cost and charges of the conveyance of the mail matter across the Atlantic. That was a British service, with the cooperation of Canada, and the contract was made with the British Government, so that they became the purveyors of the contract, so to speak. That has not been satiffactory, in so far as the proportion taxed and collected on mail matter is concerned, the British post office getting almost entirely the whole of the receipts, as it was the car-

rier between Canada and Great Britain. That contract therefore was discontinued, but the contention between the post offices was not carried to a conclusion. Meanwhile the Canadian Pacific railway carried on the service, and an arrangement was made by which the British Government assented to the old contract being continued for a year until the matters in dispute could be negotiated and settled. That time is now up, and the question of the service on the Pacific assumes a new aspect. In the meantime, the two Empresses, the Empress of Britain and the Empress of Japan, very good vessels with a speed of about eighteen knots, have been supplemented by two vessels, the Empress of Asia and the Empress of Russia, which are, taken all in all, the finest and best appointed steamships on the Pacific. We propose entering into a contract with the Canadian Pacific railway for that service for a period of three years, the two new Empresses being added to the fleet. The service was commenced as a monthly service, and it came afterwards to be a three-weekly service in the summer season. It is now proposed to put a fortnightly service between Vancouver and Victoria and Yokohama and China. There is a statutory subsidy amounting to $120,000 that is available, and this sum of $229,000 is asked for in addition, in order that a sufficient subsidy may be given for the maintenance of the service. The service on the Pacific ocean is a very important one, and at the same time very expensive. The boats on this service are the equivalent, if not. the superior, of any vessels on any Canadian service, either on the Atlantic or on the Pacific. After considering the -matter as thoroughly as possible, it was considered best to ask for this amount. As I have said, the amount provided here w-ill not be exceeded, and possibly we may be able to arrange a contract for something -less. I think it would be a very great detriment if our service with China and Japan, or the East generally, were -to be allowed to lapse. It certainly cannot be carried on without a sufficient subsidy. Under this arrangement all the proceeds from the carriage of mail matter of all kinds will come into the revenues of Canada, and will not be diverted, as under the preceding contract, into the revenues of Great Britain. It is impossible to calculate just what the revenue will be under these changed conditions, but perhaps my hon. friend the Postmaster General will be able to give
more information in that respect; but if is hoped that, with the accession of a fortnightly service of an excellent class of boats, the revenues will be very materially increased. If I were to indulge in an estimate, I should say that, under the new conditions, the revenue which would accrue to Canada would come very close to meeting the amount of the subsidy, if it did not equal or surpass it.

I agree with my hon. friend that the Pacific service is of the greatest importance, and that the relations between this country and the East are going to be multiplied to an extent which we have hardly any conception of at the present time. The Asiatics, who have -been slumbering for ages, are at l-ast awakening, and are gradually approximating to western civilization; and, unless all calculations are wrong, there will be an ever-growing trade between Europe and Asia, of which Canada ought to have her share. Up to the present time we have not had our share of the mail carried between China and England, for the reason, as I have always understood, that the Peninsular and Oriental service is quicker than our own; and, unless we can shorten our service by one, two or three days, we cannot have much hope in that direction. I believe it is possible that the service by the Canadian route may be made shorter than the service by way of the Suez canal. My hon. friend must take into consideration that by and by there will be a service between Canada and Asia via Prince Rupert, which will also ibe a shorter service. I have no doubt that at some time a demand will be made for a subsidy to that service, and I hope my hon. friend will be prepared to grant it. I would therefore urge him not to tie his hands for too long a time under the contract he has in contemplation. I would like to ask whether this $229,000 is in addition to the statutory service?
Yes.
And whether the British Government is withdrawing its allowance for that service?
Yes.
That will make a bigger outlay for us.

I just want to say a word or two on this matter and it is this; How can we go on encouraging trade between Canada and Asia and then hope to prevent' Asiatics from coming into our country? We are making the people of Asia more familiaT with Canada through having the very best steamship communication and by developing trade, and it is proposed to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars every year to encourage trade and travel between the two countries, and then we say to the Asiatic: You can buy our goods, we want to develop trade with you, but you shall not be allowed to set foot on our territory. That is going to be a troublesome question, and it is already giving this Government and the whole empire a great deal of trouble. Perhaps the time has arrived when, in the interests of Canada, we should consider whether it would not be better to discourage trade between the two countries rather than otherwise. You cannot have trade without intercourse between the peoples, and splendid steamship communication without having the people of Canada visit Asia and the people

of Asia visit Canada; and as the Asiatics become better acquainted with the splendid possibilities of our country it is only natural that they should want to share in those possibilities. It does seem to me that we are acting in a most inconsistent manner. We are spending millions to encourage the thing which we say is going to be detrimental to Canada! I think we should consider this matter very seriously before we start in to encourage intercourse between the two peoples by the expenditure of this large amount of money; that is, if we really and honestly believe-as we profess to believe whenever the question comes up-that it is against the we! fare of this country to have Asiatics come in and take advantage of the opportunities which it affords.
I am myself inclined to think thaL it f were honestly and sincerely of the opinion that Asiatics should not be permitted to come into the country and settle, it wou.d be better for us to take a firm stand and say we are not going to encourage travel, traffic, trade or intercourse between Canada and these countries, I am not so sure which would be the better course to pursue, but I do say that to pursue the two courses is very inconsistent.
Mr. MICHAEL CLARK; I think this is a very important matter for consideration. The fact is that on this question the Government seems to be a Government of limited truck and trade. In the case of our friends to the south of us, they are very glad to see the Americans but they shy at their business, while in the cage of the Asiatics they are very glad to do business but they shy at the Asiatics. So I say they are a Government of limited truck and trade. They make a most peculiar distinction to which, when we get into the recess, I invite the minister to devote his attention. This is a very abstruse problem, and it is one of those problems that we would have thought he would have devoted a great deal of attention to during the leisure he had on board ship. If he has not had time to study it in all its aspects, I respectfully ask him to see if he cannot during the recess level this thing up, find out exactly where the Government stand and give us a clear statement of it. I sympathize very much with the view of my hon. friend in front of me (Mr. Pugsley), that it will be difficult to encourage business with the Asiatics when you say that they must not come in themselves.

What do the members

from British Columbia think of this? Do they care to see these ships in the harbours there? I would like to hear from them.

My hon. friends seem to
be harassed with a distressing anxiety in this respect. Now, really, at this stage of the session-
Mr. PUG8LEY: What stage?

-do they propose to raise and settle the whole question as to immigration into Canada? The last words of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) inclined me to think that he had not taken yet the stern resolve, and that he did not think that this matter could be disposed of-
We are anxious to hear your views.

Yes, there is a proper anxiety to hear the views of one who can satisfy the desires of hon. gentlemen in that respect. There may be a little suspicion lurking in the minds of hon. gentlemen as to whether I may be able to satisfy these demands or not, but I can see by the expression of their countenances that I am quite warm-quite close-to the thought which is in their mind. I do not imagine that any Victorian, or Vancouverite, would feel sorry to see such vessels as the Empress of India, the Empress of Japan, the Empress of Asia, or the Empress of Russia, come into his port and go out again carrying products from our country paid for by the people of the East and bringing the produce of the East paid for by ourselves. If I had time to discuss it, I should immediately take issue with the statement that if you could not give British citizenship to any country in the world you should put up a prohibitive barrier and declare that there should be no traffic or transport between that country and Canada. I can conceive it to be quite possible that multitudes and multitudes of people in the East might produce what we want, send it here and accept our drafts in return, and that we could do the same with respect to them without it being necessary for gentlemen like the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to take up their residence in some of these far-off eastern countries and becoming citizens of those countries. Likewise, I think we could do quite a trade with China and Japan even without Yuan Shi Ki becoming a citizen of Montreal or acquiring certain rights as respects residence and
citizenship. But we have not time to discuss these questions at this stage. I think we agree at the present time as to the importance of the lines of transport which we have on the Pacific, even though people may be anxious with respect to that as governments and statesmen are about problems at the present time. In the meantime, as for my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), I will try and clear my impressions during the coming recess and come to certain conclusions that we may talk about when we meet here again.

I would remind the hon.
Minister of Trade and Commerce that when his Estimates in connection with the set-vices of the Trade- and Commerce Department wrere before the House on a former occasion we had some discussion in regard to the amount and progress of trade with China and Japan. Be was good enough to give a carefully worded statement as to the prospects of trade between Canada and these countries. I asked him to give the details as to the progress Canada was making and he referred me to the reports of his department. I went to the distribution office but I 'was not able to get the report of the department for the immediately preceding year, and I was therefore compelled to content myself with the report down to 1912. I have the report for 1912 before me and I think it would be desirable that the House should be informed as to the facts of the case. I must say that they do not at all bear out what my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce said in regard to the progress of trade between these countries nor do they justify an increased subsidy, to steamships running between Canada and these countries if the purpose of the subsidy is an increase of trade. I find at page 104 of the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for 1912 a statement of the trade with China and I find that the exports of Canadian produce to China in that year amounted to $413,899. In 1910 they amounted to $1,249,189. I gather that our trade is decreasing and not increasing. It was just one-fihird in 1912 of what it was in 1910. It is in the exports of Canadian produce to China that we are interested and it is the development of the trade that makes it worth our while to put up money to facilitate traffic between these countries. If the exports of Canadian produce to China are decreasing at the rate of 300 per cent in two years there should be a readjustment either of the methods of trade whereby we will get that increase that we are looking

for or else it is a matter for consideration as to how far Canada can afford to go in the matter of subsidizing steamship communications that produce such very unsatisfactory results. In 1894 the export of Canadian produce to China was $507,000, considerably more than in 1912, and in 1897 it was $761,000. The record of my hon. friend's own department is absolutely contrary to the impression that he desired to leave with the Houseonthebeeasion to which I have alluded. In the report of our trade with Japan., at page 192, I find that the exports of Canadian produce to Japan in 1912 amounted to $486,441, and that in 1910 they amounted to $659,118. The decrease is not as serious in the case of Japan as in the case of China, but still it is a decrease. In 1905, Canadian produce was sold in Japan to the amount of $508,609, and in 1912, $486,441. My point is, that when the Government is asking for an increased subsidy to improve and facilitate communication, and presumably trade communication, with these countries, it is for the Government to show that in their policy and administration they are securing results from the increased expenditure. But when we find the results as shown, I am bound to say that the demand of the Government for increased appropriations to give improved steamship service, lacks sound foundation,, if we are to consider that these moneys are voted in the interest of the people of 'Canada. Of course, if they are in the interest of a steamship company, that is a different matter. On the returns, the trade policy of my hon. friend is condemned and his application for an increased subsidy has no justification.

Two years have passed
since the statistics which my hon. friend has at his command, were published, but I have had a return made for the period between, the end of 1912 and within a few months of the present date, which I shall be happy to send to the hon. gentleman. He will see from it that the latest statistics give a better showing, and that particularly during the last ten months the development of trade with both countries has been more favourable. It must be recollected that the years 1912 and 1913 have been troubled years in China, and that consequently it is .not fair to take the statistics of trade for these years as indicative of what would be the general trend.

The conditions in Japan were not parallel with those in China, and

in Japan our sales were $486,441, as against $616,230 in the previous year, $659,118 the year before, and $756,033 in 1909. While there has been this decrease, we bought from Japan in 1912, $1,689,443 worth, as against $1,173,171 in the previous year, $987,276 in 1910, and $746,017 in 1909. While our purchases from Japan are continually increasing from 1909 to 1912, our exports to Japan have been correspondingly decreasing. My hon. friend is now asking the 'House for a vote of $229,000 in addition to the subsidy already given for a service between Canada and China and Japan, and that amount is just about one-half the value of Canada's total exports to either of these countries. Therefore, the subsidy which we give for steamship facilities is out of all proportion to the trade done. I do not wish to make any carping criticism, but the figures of our trade with these countries demonstrate as plain as day that there is something wrong with the policy of the hon. gentleman, or with the conditions upon which the policy is applied.
Steam service on the Petitcodiac river, between Moncton and way ports, and a port or ports on the west coast of Cumberland county, additional amount, $500.
How long has this subsidy been in existence?
I think for five or six years.

When the Main Estimates were under consideration, I urged that a subsidy should be given to a river service on the Mira river. It has always been contended that it was not the policy of any Government to subsidize river boats, but here we are giving a subsidy for a service on the Petitcodiac river. Has the minister given consideration to my suggestion that there should be a subsidy for the service on the Mira river?

During this summer consideration will be given to the service mentioned by the hon. member. The Petitcodiac river runs to Moncton, and my hon. friend will notice that this includes a Bay of Fundy service as well.
I hope the Government will not urge against the Mira river service that it is only a river service?

We will get all the facts during the coming summer.
Steam service between Port Mulgrave, St. Peter's, Irish Cove, and Marble Mountain, and

other ports on the Bras D'Or lakes, further amount, $500.
Are the same people doing this service?
Yes, the 8500 extra is given because they make two additional stops.
What new stops were made?
Two calls a week are made at River Bourgeois.
Does the steamer stop now at Big Pond Centre?

The same as last year.
Steam service between Pelee island and the mainland-further amount required, $3,000.
Will the minister explain the reason for this large increase?

That is the service which has long been in existence and which is a very important one, between the southwest portion of Ontario and Pelee island, which is disjoined from the main coast. There is quite a large population there, and a subsidy of $5,000 a year has been given up to the previous time. The boat, however, that was performing this service, was of rather poor quality. This year the people of the island joined with some people on the mainland and built a new steamer costing $70,000, which is now to go on the service. It is therefore considered only fair to 'increase the subsidy to $8,000. A greater number of trips are being made, and the service is infinitely superior to what- the old boat could give.
What is the population of the island?
I would not like to say definitely, but I think about 1,500 people.

I think the minister, after consideration, will agree that, for an island in lake Erie, containing a population of 1,500 people, and quite close to the mainland, $5,000 is a petty good subsidy. That has been the subsidy for a considerable time. It is now proposed in the Supplementary Estimates to increase it to $8,000. As my hon. friend the Minister of Finance would say, it synchronizes with the Ontario elections which are just coming on. I do not suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has anything to do with the synchronization; but these extraordinary events, which synchronize one with the other, aTe rather calculated to
make us sit up and take notice. Here we find that this subsidy to a small island in lake Erie, with only 1,500 people, as the minister says, has been suddenly increased from $5,000 to $8,000.

My hon. friend must take into consideration that this is a service which is performed most all the year round that the contractors carry the mails for this service as well, and that they have at certain times of the navigation to carry the mails over the ice, much the same as between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. There is no ground for the suspicion of my hon. friend that, because there is a synchronization, there is also a motive. This matter was decided upon and the contractors were given notice that it would be recommended some three months ago. It was only within a very short period that we had notice of the election.
Or suspected the election.

I can assure my hon. friend there was not the slightest thought of that in the mind of the department, which is impersonal in these' things.
Steam service between St. John, Digby, Annapolis and Granville, that is to say, along the west coast of Annapolis basin-further amount required, $500.
What is this for ?

This amount of $500 is to be added to the present subsidy of $1,500, making a total of $2,000. The contractors are the Valley Steamship Company, Limited. They asked for an increase of $1,000, but 1 did not consider that that increase should be given. Taking into consideration, however, the service of the boat and 'the general statement which the company made, I came to the conclusion that they deserved a slight increase. I think my hon. friend will agree with me in regard to that, if he looks over the statement.
Steam service between St. John, Westport, and Yarmouth and other way ports-further amount required, $3,000.

Will that include the
service performed now by the Prince George?

No, that is entirely different. These are the services which were performed last year by the Insular Steamship Company, Limited. This item is for a service which was very strongly lecom-mended by the Board of Trade and City Council of St. John. The number of trips is being largely increased. The contractors

are making steamship connections between the Nova Scotia end of the service and various other ports on the Nova Scotia coast. They have also made through rates with the southwestern ports of Nova Scotia, which have been incorporated into the contract. Altogether I think the service has been an excellent one.
Steam service between Petite de Grat and Intercolonial terminus at Mulgrave-Further amount required, $1,000.
What is this for? *

It is an additional sum
given for the service between Petite de Grat and the Intercolonial terminus at Mulgrave. The increase is given because the service is a very difficult one. It is a return trip every day in the year except Sundays, and so is not what you may call a seasonal service. I took into consideration the financial statement made by the company, and it came out in the end that the contractor would have been unable to carry on the service unless some additional subsidy were given.
What amount were they getting the year before?

$6,000. The contractor is
Mr. William G. Leslie.
Steam service between Halifax and west coast of Cape Breton, calling at way ports- Further amount required, $2,000.

What are the
ports of call for this service?

Mulgrave, Hawkesbury,
Hastings, Havre au Bouche, Port Hood, Maboumouth, Margaree, Grand Etang, Cheti-camp, Eastern Harbour, Pleasant Bay.

Is the boat supposed
to make one trip a week, and does she call at all these ports every trip ?

Not every trip, I think.
She calls every two weeks at Havre au Bouche and Margaree. It is exactly the same as last year.

Margaree is one of the most important ports on the whole route. If the provision for a call every two weeks was in last year's contract, I was not aware of_ it, and I am sure that the people of Margaree were not aware of it.

The service is a weekly
service, and, as I have it in, the report, the exception is made that she is to call every two weeks at Havre au Bouche and Margaree. Did she call weekly last year?
Yes.
If she called weekly last year, she does so this year.

The contract, then,
gives her the privilege of calling once every two weeks instead of once a week, as last year?
No, the contract has not been changed in any way as between this and last year. There may be a mistake in the explanation contained in the report, but no change in the contract has been made.

Permit me to say to the minister that there was a change as between last year and the two previous years. Why should an exception be made of the case of Margaree? Why should this boat plying along the coast and calling at all the other ports north and south cf Margaree, leave Margaree out?

I am trying to tell my
hon. friend that if under her contract the boat called at Margaree weekly last year, she will call weekly this year as well. If it is optional with the minister to say whether she shall call weekly or fortnightly, the minister will exercise his option by providing that she shall call weekly.

Very good; all I want is the minister's assurance that she will call once a week. I wish to call the attention of the minister also to the fact that during 1910 the boat plying along the coast from Mulgrave to Cheticamp had the lightering done at her own expense. I should like the minister to ask the contractors in the ease to which we have just had reference, as well as those who are in charge of the boat running from Mulgrave to Cheticamp, to pay the lightering charges themselves. It was done before, and, I think, very satisfactorily to the people. If it were not so late in the session I would consult the minister privately and explain to him the whole circumstances. The people are the sufferers when the agents are permitted to charge for landing goods; I insisted in 1910 and 1911 that the company should bear that expense.

I do not know how that
is; I will look into the matter and will give my hon. friend some information either this afternoon or to-morrow.

Is the minister
making any provision for a steamship service subsidy between the Magdalen Islands and Halifax?
No.

The Board of Trade of Halifax have frequently passed resolutions respecting this service, asking for aid. I understand that the minister has been consulted in the matter by friends of the proposed service. Has he any explanation to make?

Very full representations
were made by the Board of Trade of Halifax and by others interested in the service. The main object is to connect the Magdalen islands with the mainland and provide adequate mail and trade communication. The natural point of communication on the mainland is Pictou, from which is obtained the shortest ocean route to the islands. As the mails would have to go from Pictou anyway, it seems impossible to justify two services, one of them from Halifax, traversing a long and already frequented route.

The Magdalen Islands
do a great part of their business with Halifax.
I understand that a great deal of their trade is done with Halifax, but we are not putting on new services this year; I just note the difficulty there is in having a double service to the island.
The service is a semiweekly service, and under the same contract as before?
Yes.

I observe that no provision is made in the Estimates this year for a subsidy for the steamship service from St. John to Bear River. The minister will remember that he has frequently been asked toy the citizens and by interested parties at Bear River for restoration of the subsidy which for years had been given for steamship service between St. John and Bear River. Would the minister toe good enough to tell me frankly and sincerely why the subsidy was cut out in 1911-12?

So far as I recollect, 1
found so many services there which in the main duplicated each other that I had to do something towards having them readjusted.
Oh, no.

My recollection is not
very clear about that, but I will refresh my mind, and if my hon. friend will put the question to me some time to-day or to-morrow I will give him the exact reasons.

Will the minister be
frank?

Yes; it may not agree
with my hon. friend, tout I will give him the reasons without mental reservation.

I have no doubt in my mind that this steamship subsidy was discontinued purely for political reasons. The minister himself wrote the owner of the boat which has been plying between Beat River and St. John for years, and which, I think, is now engaged in that service, saying that if he would use the Government wharf at Bear River he would get him a subsidy. Mr. Clark, the owner, says that the wharf should never have been built, that it never was used and never will be used, and, lastly, that he himself cannot use it.

I scarcely think that I wrote a letter of that kind; but I do remember that the point was up as to whether it was not wise in all our contracts to make our subsidized steamers stop at Government wharfs where Government wharfs are available. There was some question about that particular Government wharf, but I do not think it was impossible to use it. This raises the interesting question as to who put the wharf there, if the assertion is true that it is not an available one. I think, however, we all agree that where the Government goes to the expense of building wharfs and where those wharfs are commodious and usable, our subsidized steamers should use them.

The minister says that there is a. daily service between Petite de Grat and Mulgrave. I should think that a daily service between those points would be an impossibility, particularly during a severe winter. Has the minister a report showing that daily connection is made between those points?

The contract calls for
daily return service; if they do not make the daily return service they suffer a diminution of their subsidy in proportion to the number of trips they miss. But it is destined to be a daily service. In 1913 they

made two hundred and eighty-one and a half round trips.
I understand that it calls at Arisaig, but in anything like severe weather that harbour is closed over. I would ibe very glad if these people were able to make daily trips.

The purpose is to make daily trips. Sometimes the weather is so bad that the trip cannot be made. Then they do not get the subsidy.
Steam service between Halifax and Spry Bay and ports in Cape Breton, $2,000.
What ports at Cape Breton does this vessel call at?

The vessel running from Halifax calls at the following ports in Cape Breton: St. Peters, Arisaig, West Arisaig, L'Ardoise and Margaree.
Schooner service between Pictou, New Glasgow, Antigonish county ports and Mulgrave - Further amount required, $500.
At what ports will this vessel call, and why the increase?

That service was performed last year, not by a high class steamship, but it was a very useful service intended to make connections between the ports at which the Pictou-Mulgrave service could not call on account of the shallowness of the harbours. It performed a very useful service last year, and I think I have as many commendations from the people of that coast on the convenience afforded them by that small service, perhaps more, than I had on many more pretentious services. It is proposed this year to make additional calls and to put on a better type of vessel. The boat that is to be put on has an auxiliary power. She is 62 ft. long, and has a capacity of 30 tons. In consideration of the increased calls, an additional amount of $500 is given.

At what places
will it call? I agree that, considering the character of the boat, the service was a very good one, that is, that the contractors did their duty. The unfortunate thing is that 'the haiibours there have been entirely neglected by the Minister of Public Works. Of course, we get promises from time to time, but, some way or other, the sand gathers in, the wharfs tumble down, the harbours are altogether neglected-and promises do not seem to relieve the situation. As we get near to an election, however, I have no doubt that the situation will be

%
relieved, and the service, that has deteriorated in recent years because of the neglect of the harbours, will be improved.

I shall give the ports at which she calls. They are Pictou, Lismore, McAra's Brook, Arisaig, Malignant Cove, Georgeville, Livingston Cove, Ballantyne Cove, and three other ports:
Winter steam service between St. John, Halifax and London-Further amount required, $1,500.

Upon this item which is closely related to the matter of the mail subsidy for the fast Atlantic winter mail service, I desire to ask a question of the Postmaster General. It apparently is a part of this vote. About a year ago a contract was made for the winter mail service to Great Britain, and it was a term or provision of the contract made between the Government of Canada and the contracting steamship companies that the contractors had the right of selecting their winter Atlantic ports. The Canadian Pacific railway, the Royal Mail Steamship Company, the White Star Company, and the Allan line, I think, designated Halifax as the port of departure for the fast Atlantic mail service. Later on, shortly after the winter mail service was commenced, considerable opposition arose in the city of St. John against the departure from that port of the Canadian Pacific mail boats which had been sailing to and from St. John for a great number of years. They made a strong protest to the Government. I stated, in a few remarks I addressed to the House upon this matter some time ago, that the Government has unduly interfered in the matter, and that the transference of the Royal line from Halifax to St. John was due to the interference of the Government. I rather gathered from the remarks made by the Postmaster General at that time that there had been some Government interference, and I would like to ask the Postmaster General now what is the nature of the contracts made with the steamship companies for carrying the mails during the coming winter season. Has any contract been made, and if so, is any port designated, or have the contractors the option of selecting their own ports ? I would like to know if interference is to be permitted on behalf of anybody. As a representative of the city of Halifax I desire to urge that that port be specifically mentioned in the contract as the point of departure and arrival of these .fast Atlantic mail boats.
Does my hon. friend from St. John agree with that ?
My hon. friend knows that all St. John wants is justice.
That is not an answer to my question.
Again I want to appeal to my hon. friend to defer his remarks until we get to the mail service item.

Where is it ?
Mr. FOSTER. In the Main Estimates.
Mr. MACLEAN. Will the minister say he will take that up immediately after three o'clock ?
Yes.
That will be satisfactory to me.

Before we take up the Atlantic mail service item will my hon. friend have his colleague the acting Minister of Railways give us a statement of what the freight and passengers carried under the Gutelius agreement of last year between St. John and Halifax would have netted to the Intercolonial under the then existing tariff. The return does not show that.

I will speak to the minister about it.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.
Trade and Commerce-Supervision, lake and ocean freight rates-Salary and expenses of offiial, 26,000.

What does that
mean?

In carrying on the work
of the Department of Trade and Commerce, in which we 'have numerous questions arising in reference to ocean and lake freight rates, I find that the department is very poorly -manned for that service. Freight rates, particularly ocean freight rates and all that appertains to them, is a very complex -and abstruse question and, for a man who is not experienced, it is very perplexing. In- all our contracts we have clauses which when worked out, call for the decision of the minister as to whether the freight rate is too great or too small. I find that I am not able to enter into the contest with a freight expert. I propose to have my department provided with a small staff whose business it will be to take up that work and furnish the department with the
information that is absolutely necessary for it to have before it can act. It will take up the question of freight rates on the lakes as well as oee-aan transport.

I think the proposition of the minister is a pretty fair one. I can understand that a service of that description might be very well utilized for such a purpose. Am I correct in assuming that this official will have supervision of steamers which receive a subsidy from the Government, the contract with which it provides that an approval of rates must be had from the department?
Yes.

And that he will pay
particular attention to these matters?
Yes.
Has the minister anybody in mind as the chief of this branch?

I have nobody in my
mind at all but, as far as my judgment can lead me, I want a man really efficient and expert in that kind of business wherever I can get him.

One man will be all
that you require?

One man is quite sufficient. We have clerk force enough in the office to assist him in the work. All there will be will be the salary of the official, but if we get a proper man we will have to pay him a proper salary.
Ocean and mail service between Canada and Great Britain, $1,000,000.

When the House Tose at one o'clock I had just begun a few observations respecting the contract for the Atlantic mail service, especially in the winter season and with particular reference to the Atlantic port which will be used by the contracting mail boats. In the contract of last year between the Government and the contracting steamship companies there was a provision that the power of selecting the port should be with the contracting steamship companies. The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), at the last session of Parliament, was clear and pronounced in saying that the contracting steamship companies would absolutely possess the power of selecting the ports of landing and embarking the mails, and he also expressed the opinion that this was a fair proposal. At the time I did not oppose this particular part of the contract,

because I thought there was a great deal to be said in favour of leaving the selection of the port to the contractors. I think that was the view of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), who with myself represents the constituency of Halifax, which constituency has been, and now is, considerably interested in the ports utilized by the subsidized mail boats during the winter season. While there was a feeling of disappointment at Halifax that the practice which had prevailed for thirty-six years, namely, the landing and embarking of the mails at Halifax, was not to be continued, yet there was a disposition, I think, not to regard that feature of the contract as entirely unfair. I think the friends of the port of Halifax felt that if that port had merits superior to those of other ports they would 'be recognized by the contracting steamship companies and the best port would be selected. If any contracting steamship company had selected a port other than Halifax, it might have been urged, as it was and with some fairness, that Halifax would have to submit to the selection made. The mail contract, as I Tecollect, was divided among four steamship companies-the Allan, Canadian Pacific railway, Canadian Northern and White Star lines. I think that under the terms of the contract all of these contracting companies made a selection of the port of Halifax. It soon became quite obvious and notorious that after the designation of the port of Halifax by the contracting steamship companies tremendous influence and pressure was being exerted upon the Government to induce some of the contractors to adopt St. John as a port for landing and embarking the Atlantic mails.
I think that the selection of Halifax by the contracting companies was deliberate and for cause. I believe they had a preference for that port, and I think that the contracting steamship companies would have used the port of Halifax entirely during the past winter season had it not been for government interference. I do not want to take up any time in reiterating the statement that there was interference by the Government. I believe there was. It may foe quite true that there is no evidence of concrete governmental action, but I am satisfied beyond any doubt 'whatever that there was active and effective iater-ference on the part of members of the Government. The interference was designed for a purpose, which was accomplished. I

do not propose accepting the denials of the Government in respect to this matter.
By reason of this interference, the Canadian Northern Railway Company particularly was forced to leave the port of Halifax which they had used for a number of years, and went to the port of St. John. It is quite clear that pressure was exerted upon this company because earlier in the season its vice-president publicly stated that they did not intend to leave the port of Halifax, and the president of the company, Sir William McKenzie expressed publicly his preference for that port. It is unnecessary, however, that I should attempt to prove that there was direct interference on the part of the Government. That is now an accepted fact.
We are paying one million dollars a year for the transatlantic mail service, and consequently all Canada is interested in it. The people of Canada have the right to expect the adoption by the contracting steamship companies of that port which will deliver to Canadians the transatlantic mails in the speediest manner. I submit that if the mail-boats use Halifax as their winter port, the people of all Canada would receive their mail anywhere from twelve hours to twenty-four hours earlier than if the mails were landed in any other Atlantic port. That is an undeniable fact. At the request of the Halifax Board of Trade, the Post Office Department kept a record of the sailings of the subsidized mail boats to and from the ports of St. John and Halifax during the last winter season. The Halifax Board of Trade have issued a printed memorandum based upon the information supplied by the Post Office Department. It may be said that the statement is from biased sources, but that is not important if the facts are true, as I submit they are. 1 will read the statement:
Taking the forty-three winter sailings of the Liverpool-Bristol to Montreal winter mail service, via the ports of Halifax and St. John, it is found from the official returns furnished by the Postmaster General that the average advantage per trip via Halifax is twelve hours and forty-three minutes over St. John in the time consumed from United Kingdom ports to Montreal.
The tabulated returns have been furnished by Postmaster General Pelletier as promised to the Board of Trade. While St. John had the greater number of fast boats, still Halifax was easily able to demonstrate its superiority as a port for the speedy transportation of the mails.
The tabulation shows 23 sailings from Liverpool to Montreal via Halifax and 21 sailings Bristol-Liverpool to Montreal via St. John.
The Halifax sailings collectively consumed 202 days and 15 hours, which gave an average

for each of the 23 Halifax sailings of 8 days, 19 hours and 11 minutes.
The 21 sailings via St. John consumed 195 days, 22 nours and 35 minutes, or an average per trip of 9 days, 7 hours and 54 minutes, thus giving an average advantage to Halifax of 12 hours and 43 minutes each trip.
Another fact is to be stated which renders this comparison more significant still. It is that while Halifax had 9 sailings of the slower boats, such as the Corsican, etc., St. John had only 4, but had 17 of the faster boats, such as the Royals, while Halifax had only 14. In spite of this Halifax beats the sister port by over half a day per trip, in point of time, between England and Montreal.
A point has been made that in all the service one trip via St. John happened to be the fastest of the whole series, but supposing this trip, which was made by the Royal George, had been via Halifax, with 270 miles less sailing, the time to Montreal would have been still further reduced.
The test has now been held and Halifax has proved herself to be the port for the fast transportation of mails. In spite of St. John having the faster boats Halifax comes out of the ordeal with a record of an average of twelve hours and forty-three minutes less time from England to Montreal than St. John.
Is that inclusive of rail?

Yes.
Mr. FOSTER- I wish for iny own information 1o ask if in making the comparison between St. John and Halifax as ports of entry, the same railway carnage is used, or a different railway carriage?

The railway carriage is
from Halifax to Montreal on the Intercolonial, and from St. John to Montreal by the Canadian Pacific railway.
They only send from St. John occasionally by the Canadian Pacific railway. That is where they gave us the double-cross; they sent us around by Moncton.
If my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) is not correct in his statements, I turn him over to the vigilant scrutiny of the bon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley).

I have no doubt we shall soon hear from both of the hon. members for St. John. I might point out that there was more or less difficulty in connection with the departure of the mails from Halifax to Montreal during the last winter season. Frequently the mails, when landed at Halifax, were not promptly forwarded to Montreal and western points for many hours afterwards. There seems to have been negligence or carelessness on the part of somebody in connection with the despatch of the mails after being landed from the boats. I believe the people of St. John 318
have a similar complaint. I understand that the Canadian Post Office Department disclaims any responsibility for the mails after they are landed, they contending that the responsibility for that rests upon the British Post Office Department. Had there been promptness in the despatch of the mails after being landed at Halifax, the average results would have been much more favourable to the port of Halifax than set forth in the memorandum of the Board of Trade of Halifax. It has been demonstrated in the past that there can be a saving of from twelve to twenty hours, and perhaps more, by receiving and despatching our European mails from the port of Halifax, as against any other Atlantic port.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman
making any allowance for the distance from Liverpool and from Bristol?

That would not matter because ships approaching the Atlantic coast of Canada, whether from Bristol or from Liverpool, pursue a certain track across the ocean until they reach a point about sixty miles off the coast of Nova Scotia, from which they diverge to St. John or Halifax as the case may be. That point is sixty miles from Halifax and 330 miles from St. John.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the distance from Bristol to that point is longer than the distance from Liverpool to that point, it would make a difference in the time consumed.

I do not think that is an element of importance, because if a ship sails from Bristol for the port of Halifax and there despatches her mails for Montreal by the Intercolonial, the same will reach Montreal and western points from twelve to twenty hours earlier than if they were landed at the port of St. John and from there despatched to Montreal. Inasmuch as we are paying $1,000,000 for this service, the port of landing the mails should be that which will give Canadians their European mails in the quickest possible time. That is a matter of ordinary business, and I cannot see how my position can safely be controverted by any one. One might also refer to the preference of the ship-owners, the safety of ships and the safety of passengers. The preference of the contracting steamship companies should receive special consideration for these reasons. In my judgment, Halifax has special advantages as a winter mail port over any other port in the Maritime provinces. I



believe it is the desire and the wish of the contractors to adopt Halifax as the winter port, and I submit it was unfair and unjust to that port that any interference should have been made by the Government in the direction of inducing the contractors to change from one port to another when under the contract they had made their selection of ports. We have had an experience with permitting the contractors to designate their port, and have found that they afterwards were not permitted to carry out their selection. For that reason I have no confidence that the contractors will be given a free hand in selecting a port. I desire to urge upon the Postmaster General and the Government that the port of Halifax should be designated in the contract as the port of landing and embarking the ocean mails. I fear that, if the contract in this respect is to be as last year, there will be further political interference. Consequently there is no advantage in leaving in the contract the right of selection by the contractors.

Although a debate on this question naturally takes rather a local flavour, it is, I think, of such importance as to call for the earnest attention of the committee. The matter of improved fast Atlantic steamship service is one which has been in the public mind for a great many years, and is associated always with the mail service. Ever since I was a boy I have heard it discussed. Sometimes it appeared near and then it appeared to recede as we apparently approached its establishment.
As we have devoted so much attention and such large sums of money to the provision of a land transportation system, the development which should naturally follow is the fast Canadian Atlantic service and which should be encouraged in every way possible. We have gone the limit in giving assistance to land transportation companies. Every hon. member is thoroughly seized of the fact that the obligations which have been undertaken in this connection have been exceedingly large. One of the largest undertakings and for which tremendous obligations have been assumed was for the avowed and express purpose of providing ourselves with a system which began at a Canadian port and ended at a Canadian port, a transcontinental road all on Canadian territory and using Canadian ports. That was the alluring picture drawn at the time that the most expensive

transportation system that we have up to the present secured was launched. Therefore, I submit that, in considering the transportation of mails, that point should be borne in mind. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) the other day referred to a proposal to carry these mails over American territory. I would submit -and in this I am sure the right hon. the leader of the Opposition will agree with me -that that is not a proposal which should be considered; that we should if possible -and we can-be independent in regard to the transportation of mails as well as in regard to the transportation of freight- have a self-contained mail carrying system in Canadian territory and using Canadian ports. During the first session for which I had the honour of sitting in this House, I took occasion to bring to the attention of Parliament this matter of improved fast Atlantic steamship service. At that time my argument was on all fours with that of my hon.. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) namely, that in the selection of a Canadian port there should be no discrimination; that a fast Atlantic line should be encouraged to establishment, and that the best port should be selected on its merits. I was particularly pleased, when the new mail contract was being made, that the matter of the selection of the port was left entirely in the hands of the contractors.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has already read a statement prepared by the Halifax Board of Trade, which is based on official information given out by the Postmaster General. It seems to me that the improvement or advance which has been made in the mail service has not been at all satisfactory. The amount of subvention voted for this service has been augmented by some $400,000, and the opinion is expressed in many well-informed quarters that the mail service given to this country last winter was really inferior to the service enjoyed in previous years and under previous contracts.
Does my hon. friend mean that the Canadian service was better in previous years ?

The statement has been put forward by people who do a large transatlantic business and depend largely on the mails in the prosecution thereof, that the service given during the past year has not been any improvement on the service

given under previous contracts and with a much lower subsidy; at any rate, so far as the interests of my personal business friends residing in Nova Scotia are concerned, they state the deliveries of mail have been slower this past winter than in previous years.
I should like to point out to my hon. friend that the service last year was a Canadian service while the service during the year previous was a foreign service.

Voyages were made last winter under the mail contract by vessels which should not have been used for the carrying of mails under the contract. They were old and slow years ago, and their names are more familiar to our fathers than to us.
It does not seem to me that a case has been made out along the line of the argument put forward by the hon. gentleman who has just sat down. It is quite true that during the last winter there was in the city of Halifax quite a little disappointment, and some surprise, when the 'Canadian Northern boats were withdrawn from Halifax and sent to another port; but no proof has been adduced, ,so far as I am aware, that this proposal was not made by the Canadian Northern people, the proprietors of this steamship line. Referring to the matter from a purely local standpoint, in some business circles in Halifax it was looked upon as a blessing in disguise that these boats did not come to that port during the last winter. The. terminal facilities and equipment for handling these steamers were stated to be insufficient, and well-posted shipping men have made the statement that had all the shipping gone to Halifax last winter there would have been difficulty in taking care of it.
Previous to last year there was great congestion at deep water, and I am informed by shipping men that if the additional boats to which the hon. gentleman refers had gone there last year, it is very questionable whether the business could have been properly taken care of.
When the hon. gentleman, asserts that no interference or pressure should be brought to bear on contractors in the selection of ports, I am entirely at one with him.
Those who are acquainted with the waterfront at Halifax know that for many years past there has been a considerable congestion of traffic. Representations were 3184
made by representatives of the board of trade in that city urging that the terminal facilities should be augmented in a comprehensive manner. It had always puzzled me that the Government did not take steps, not to equip the port for 'business that *might offer in the future, but to provide an equipment sufficient to cope with existing business. As responsible for the operation of the Intercolonial railway, the Government should certainly provide the facilities necessary to handle business pressing on the road.
I state no more than the fact when I say that the facilities there were quite incapable of coping with the business offered, and that as a consequence delay and loss frequently occurred. And frequent and urgent representatives for relief received little response from the Government. Any hon. gentlemen who are inclined to question this assertion may refer to the delegations which visited Ottawa to impress the existing state of affairs upon ^he Government. They finally did receive as a compromise the undertaking that another additional wharf would be built; this wharf, which is now in course of construction and almost completed, is known as No. 2. While hon. gentlemen are inclined tc be critical and even to censure the Government for disappointments which occur in the development of a promising business, with a desire to be fair I wish to say that the business community of Halifax learned with a great deal of satisfaction of the attitude of the present Government with regard to the transportation question, and have considerable confidence in the ultimate working out by the Government of the important eastern transportation problem.
While transportation systems were being built up across the continent, sufficient attention was not being paid to the facilities for transhipment when this traffic reached tidewater. Although this pressing state of affairs was brought earnestly to the attention of the predecessors of the present Government, they received scant recognition and nothing of a comprehensive character was undertaken until the present Government came into office.
Extensive plans for the accommodation of the trade to which I have referred are now being carried out, and they are so regarded as an earnest of the present Administration's intention to handle the problem in a comprehensive manner that I think the

business community of that city have not felt much concern, or been disposed to become alarmed over the temporary withdrawal of 'boats by the Canadian Northern railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At this late stage of the
'session I shall not occupy very much of the time of the House in a discussion of this matter; but at the same time I feel that, as a representative of the constituency of St. John, I should not allow the remarks made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), which are undoubtedly an. attack upon the capacity and merit of St. John as a mail port, to go unanswered. The respective merits of the ports of Halifax and St. John as mail ports have been matters of discussion for a good many years past. I have always thought it would be better, in the interests of both ports, if there was less discussion of their respective merits, less attempt to cry down one or the other, and if there was more union between them with a view to advancing the interests of the lower province ports and of the lower provinces generally. At the same time those people who are interested in the port and business of St. John, have contended for years that the winter mails to and from Canada could be handled with just as much expedition through St. John as through any other port in the lower provinces. As my hon. friend has pointed out, for a period of about thirty-six years the mail contracts provided that the carriers of the mails were to receive and deliver them at the port of Halifax and thus, for all those years, there was no opportunity for the port of St. John to demonstrate by actual experience whether the claims made by its citizens that it was in a position to successfully compete with Halifax as a mail port were or were not correct. Last year a contract was entered into by the Postmaster General for the carriage of the mails. That contract provided that in the winter season the carriers of the mail should, on their own option, select the port in Canada on the Atlantic seaboard at which they would deliver and receive the mails, and the Postmaster General undertook to deliver the mail to them at the port of Halifax or of St. John. That was the policy of the open door for which citizens of St. John have contended, and with reason I think, for a great many years past. I can see no possible objection to leaving the carriers of the mads free to select the port of departure. It certainly seems to me that that is a fair proposition,

fair to Halifax and fair to St. John, because the carrier of the mail will naturally be influenced by the merits of the ports and their facilities for the handling and rapid distribution of the mails throughout the country. My hon. friend has said that there was pressure brought to bear because the Canadian Northern railway boats, the Royal George and the Royal Edward, left Halifax and came to St. John, last winter. I think that my hon. friend ought to bear in mind that the Canadian Pacific railway and the Allan line steamers announced through the press that all their boats would sail direct from St. John to Liverpool. After that announcement in the press they changed their minds and went to Halifax as the Canadian Northern railway later changed their minds. Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, explaining this action on behalf of the Canadian Pacific railway, stated most emphatically that St. John was the port of the Canadian Pacific railway, that their action in taking the Empresses to Halifax last year was merely tentative and that they proposed to return to St. John as soon as there were facilities there so as to enable them to properly handle the freight, mail and passenger business. We in St. John certainly have just as much right to complain of the change on the part of the Canadian Pacific railway -as my hon. friend has to -complain because of the Change of the Canadian Northern railway in bringing the Royal boats to St. John.

Oh, no. There is this distinction. The Canadian Pacific Railway boats selected Halifax, under the contract, of their own volition and not at the suggestion of the Government. The Prime Minister himself publicly stated that this was the act of the Canadian Pacific railway. But I say, and I mean it and I h-ave reason for knowing it, that pressure was brought to bear on the Canadian Northern railway by members of the Government. It is not a guess with me at all.

speechtext:
That shows the difficulty of making comparisons or drawing conclusions from such a statement as my hon. friend has read to the House. No doubt
