there are individual cases in which the mail from Halifax has been delivered quicker than from St. John, and vice versa. Looking at it from that standpoint, and taking into consideration the fact that the mails through St. John were hauled in some cases by the longer land route from St. John and by the longer water route from Bristol, I think it will be admitted that mails can be handled through St. John with as much expedition as they can through Halifax.
I would like to read to the House a statement from a circular letter of the St. John Board of Trade under date 29th May,. 1914:
The statement of mail records as between the ports of St. John and Halifax, which was compiled by the Post Office Department, while it may be employed to substantiate the claim of St. John to mail carrying supremacy, is not sufficiently clear upon a very important point to justify any dependable comparisons being made. It does not in every instance refer to mails which were despatched over the shorter rail route from St. John to Montreal over the Canadian Pacific railway. In some instances, the time of haulage from this port to Montreal was over the longer Intercolonial Railway route instead of over the shorter route. The unfairness of making a comparison of the relative merits of Maritime province ports, based upon such a condition as the above, can readily be seen.
I am sure this must appeal to the sense of fairness of my hon. friend from Halifax The statement continues:
It is interesting to note in connection with the official record, that the palm for the fastest delivery of mails during the past winter was carried off by the port of St. John.
This was in the case of the Royal George, which arrived in St. John on January 7, and whose mails reached Montreal in twenty-two minutes less than any mail shipment from any other Maritime mail port. This incident affords a striking example of the superiority of St. John in this connection.
The result of the experience of the past winter-which is supported by the incomplete official record-shows that St. John has every right to be considered on equal terms with any other mail port that may be seeking recognition.
I think that is a very correct summing up of the case. In the contract which will be entered into, I understand that St. John will be considered on an equal footing with any other mail port on the Atlantic coast that is seeking recognition. The selection of the port will be left to the contractors themselves, and consequently I do not think any port has any right to find fault or to demand, as my hon. friend has demanded for Halifax, that it shall be named in the contract to the exclusion of all other ports. Such a course would be manifestly unfair.
	.
Let the policy of the ' open door ' prevail. Each port will stand on its own merits, but having regard to the fact as stated in the communication of the Toronto Board of Trade that there is very little difference between Halifax and St. John so far as the delivery of the English mail in Toronto is concerned, the result may be that the service will be divided between the two ports. That matter, however, is in the hands of the contractors. I do not see how any port can fairly find fault with an arrangement of this sort under which each port stands on its merits and will be considered on its merits alone, and under which the contractor is given power to decide on the port which will be most advantageous from his standpoint.

Is it the intention to
renew the rather famous and much attacked Gutelius-Bosworth agreement, being an agreement between the Government railways of which Mr. Gutelius is general manager and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think there has been any decision to renew that particular agreement in its actual terms. No doubt negotiations will be carried on between the Government and the Canadian Pacific railway with regard to access to Halifax for such of its boats as may be run there.

I am very glad indeed to observe how completely my hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Hazen) has answered my hon. friend from Halifax as to the respective merits of Halifax and St. John as mail ports. The sooner the Government recognize that those two ports have merits and settle this difference of the mail service between the two ports by dividing the fast mail steamers equally between them the better it will be for both ports. It is not desirable, it is not in the public interest, that this jealousy should continue and that the people of either port should not know what to expect. If the subsidy is to be given year after year, if it is to be voted by Parliament, and if then the matter is to be left optional with the steamship companies, they will play off one port against the other, just as they are doing to-day. The longshoremen who serve the steamers, loading and unloading, will not know what to expect. We had a very distressing example, as a result of the uncertainty, in what has taken place in St. John during the last winter. For a good many years past the winter port business

has been steadily increasing, and quite a large number of longshoremen have had steady employment. It was expected that last winter the Empress steamers would come to St. John as usual. They did not come, and the result was that for the first time in the history of the winter port business, St. John had a large number of people who were thrown out of employment, and a rather distressing state of affairs occurred. The matter ought to be settled. If these fast steamers are to be subsidized for the winter service, three of them ought to be subsidized for St. John and three for Halifax. That would make two trips a week. Let there be one from Halifax and one from St. John. If it could be arranged definitely and permanently that each port was to get a part of the service, then each port could go ahead with its development of business, knowing what to expect in the future.
My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries rather favoured the idea that the same agreement is to be made with the companies as that which was made last winter. He called attention to the fact that there was general satisfaction with the proposal to allow an open door. If I remember rightly, last session I suggested the same thing that I am suggesting now, that the service should be equally divided, but the Government thought it well to take this course, although the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) gave the most positive assurance that each port would be treated with absolute fairness. The Postmaster General was speaking for the Government when he said that. We cannot separate the different departments of the Government. Whatever one minister does is the act of the Government for which the whole Government is responsible. Whatever the deputy head of a department does is the act of the whole Government and the whole Government is responsible.
What took place after this agreement was entered into? The Canadian Pacific railway having the terminus of their railway at the port of St. John, made up their mind that they would make St. John the port for their mail steamers. The Canadian Pacific railway, as is generally known, control the Allan line steamers as well. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries says that lists of sailings were prepared and inserted in the newspapers and notices were also sent out inviting tenders from grocers and other supply men for supplying the
Empress steamers at the port of St. John. Almost immediately after these advertisements appeared there came an announcement that the Canadian Pacific railway had changed their plans altogether and that they were going to make Halifax the terminus of their mail steamers. Mr. Bosworth, the gentleman who signed the agreement, to which I shall refer a little later, on behalf of the Canadian Pacific railway, and who, I believe, is the general traffic manager of that road, made a statement in an interview' published in the Montreal papers that the Canadian Pacific railway had decided to send their steamers direct to St. John because they were not able to make a sufficiently favourable arrangement with the Intercolonial railway. But he said that they had, within a few days, completed arrangements which were entirely satisfactory, and that they had therefore, changed their mind and that the steamers were going to stop at Halifax The people of St. John were naturally very much surprised and I think I can say, on behalf of the people of St. John, that they have no desire to in any way interfere with the legitimate ambitions of their sister city of Halifax. They would like to see Halifax grow and develop and become one of the great cities of Canada. But they want to be treated fairly and to be treated on an equality with other portions of Canada. When they found that the effect of the arrangement which the Government had made with the Canadian Pacific railway, was to induce the Canadian Pacific railway not to use the open door which the Postmaster General had announced would be afforded to them they naturally became very indignant, sought to ascertain why it was that this agreement had been entered, into and endeavoured to have it revoked. I may say that they learned of this agreement some weeks before it was to go into operation. It was made on the 30th of September and it was to go into operation on the 15th of November, so that there was in the period between the 30th of September and the 15th of November ample time for the matter to be considered by the Government. Immediately upon the people of St. John learning of it in the month of October they called upon the Government to reconsider it. They had meetings and resolutions of the board of trade and Government supporters in the city of St. John, men of great prominence, took the platform and alleged that i.f this iniquitous agree-

ment was allowed to go into force there would be the greatest split in the Conservative party that had been seen in St. John for a long time. A delegation was sent to Ottawa; the Prime Minister will remember it. It was headed by the president of the board of trade, and the people of St. John took the very reasonable ground that the Government should not, as the owners and operators of the Intercolonial railway, make an agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway to give them rates more favourable than those which existed before and therefore induce them to change their plans, deter them from selecting St. John as the port which they had decided upon and cause them to make Halifax the terminus of their mail steamers. I remember that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) said that St. John might depend upon it that the Government w'ould not allow any discrimination against St. John or any other port. In view of that I was greatly surprised to hear the Minister of Marine and Fisheries say not long ago in this House when I had the honour to mention this subject, that he did not know whether the agreement was discriminatory against St. John, that Mr. Gutelius, the general manager, said it was not and that the rates now given to the Canadian Pacific railway had been given by the Government some years ago to the Canadian Northern.	Noth withstanding all the protests which were made, that agreement was allowed to go into effect. It had to be approved of by the Government, or the Minister of Railways and Canals, and I hold the Government and every member of the Government responsible for the agreement and for its being allowed to go into operation. They cannot escape the responsibility for it. I maintain that it was an unfair act towards the port of St. John. When the vote was given by Parliament and when the open door was so boastfully offered to the people of both Halifax and St. John, it was supposed that the steamship companies would have to conform to the rates prevailing upon the Intercolonial against all shippers under similar circumstances, and that no specially favourable arrangement would be made to induce the steamship companies to abandon St. John and decide in favour of Halifax. A return was moved for at my request, which was prepared by Mr. Gutelius, the general manager, and it reads:
Return of Department of Railway by F. P. Gutelius, general manager.

Canadian Government railways, Intercolonial railway,
Moncton, N.B., April 28, 1914.
A. W. Campbell, Esq., C.E.,
Deputy Minister,
Department of Railways and Canals, Ottawa,
Dear Sir,-Your letter of April 9 asking for information to answer question of the House of Commons by Honourable Mr. Pugsley:
Question No. 1: How many passengers have been carried over the Intercolonial railway from St. John to Halifax, and from Halifax to St. John, respectively, under the agreement made on the 30th September, 1913, between the Canadian Government railways by F. P. Gutelius, general manager, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company by G. M. Bosworth, general traffic manager, from the 15th November, 1913 when the said agreement went into effect to the 31st March last?
Answer:	Number of passengers carried from
St. John to Halifax, 6,778 ; number of passengers carried from Halifax to St. John, 7,698.
Question No. 2 :	How many tons of freight
of each of the classes mentioned in said agreement have been carried each way over the Intercolonial railway between St. John and Halifax under said agreement during said period?
Answer:	Freight carried from St. John to
Halifax, flour and grain, 31,461 ; all other classes of freight, 12,804^ ; total, 44,265 tons.
Freight carried from Halifax to St. John, all classes of freight, 18,757 tons.
Question No. 3 :	What have been the total
earnings by the Intercolonial railway under said agreement up to the 31st March last for passengers and freight carried respectively?
Answer:	Total earnings for passengers carried, $25,960:	total earnings for freight,
$50,683.31 ; total, $76,643.31.
Question No. 4 :	What amount has been paid
to or earned by the Canadian Pacific railway for car hire under said agreement?
Answer:	Mileage on passenger equipment,
$3,302.75 per diem; on freight cars approximately, $5,875.20 per diem; total, $9,177.95.
Question No. 5:	What number of empty
cars of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have been hauled by the Intercolonial railway free under said agreement, and what has been the cost of such haulage?
Answer:	None.
Question No. 6 :	What would have been the
total amount paid by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to the Intercolonial railway under the tariff prevailing at the time of the making of the said agreement for the passengers and the freight so carried, respectively?
Answer:	Nothing, as there would have
been no business under the prevailing tariff and the division thereof.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) F. P. Gutelius.
The last answer is a most extraordinary answer to give to the question involved in the return. What I wanted and what was required by the question was this: Under the arrangement which was prevailing before this agreement came into force, there was a through rate and division of rates as between the Intercolonial and the steamship lines using Halifax. For inward

freight the rate between Halifax and St. John would be so much, and also between Hal.fax and Montreal so much, and that is what I wanted the Minister of Railways to tell me. Here were 63,000' tons of freight which were carried between Halifax and St. John under this unusually favourable agreement, and what I asked for was what would be paid for that quantity of freight under the tariff schedule prevailing before this agreement came into force.

Is that local
freight?	.

No, it is through freight as between the steamers and the railway. All the steamship men have it and the acting minister ought to be able to get it within ten minutes from his department. There is also a rate for passengers coming by steamship from Halifax and going to Montreal, or St. John, ot other points. I wanted to know how much the 14,000 passengers would have paid under the tariff schedule which was prevailing berore this agreement was brought into force, and as to these two matters the department has not given me the information I sought. I shall present some figures which will give the House an idea of the nature of this agreement and the favourable consideration which was given to the Canadian Pacific railway. The ordinary freight rate on lumber from St. John to Halifax is, I am told, $2.75 per ton.	_
A local rate?

No, for the 275 miles
between St. John and Halifax.
Is that an export rate?

It is the rate between
St. John and Halifax.

It is a local rate.
Mr. PUGSLEY':	It is from one Atlantic terminus of the Intercolonial railway to the other.
What is it from Montreal to Halifax?

I do not know. Every
railroad man will tell you that freight cannot be hauled on the Intercolonial for less than six-tenths of a cent per ton per mile, and at that rate it would have given for that freight alone for the number of tons carried $123,750 which the Government would have received. The ordinary first-class passenger rate between St. John
and Halifax is three cents per mile for the 275 miles, or something over eight dollars.
Does any lumber, as a matter of fact, go to Great Britain via Halifax on these Empress boats?

I do not know. As I said, there were over 14,000 passengers. For the 275 miles, the ordinary first-class passenger pays upwards of $8, the ordinary rate being three cents per mile. Of course, the second-class rate will be much less than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Will my hon. friend say that lumber was carried from St. John to Halifkx for shipment out of Halifax to Great Britain at the rate he mentioned?
I am not sure as to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think that is so, because it is a local rate.

I wanted my hon. friend, who has the tariff schedule, to give me exactly what it would be; but he has not done so, and therefore I have to argue the matter as best I can from the ordinary rate. Suppose you allow for the 14,000 passengers a dollar and a half each for carrying them 275 miles, which is a very low rate indeed, being only a little over half a cent per mile, that would make $21,000. This, plus $123,750, makes $144,750, which would have been paid by the Canadian Pacific railway as against the amount they actually paid of $76,643.31. The freight charges to them were about three-tenths of a cent per ton per mile. No railway man will tell you that freight can be hauled on the Intercolonial railway for anything like that rate, because my information is that six-tenths of a cent per ton is the average cost per mile. What we in St. John complain of bitterly is that the Canadian Pacific ought to have been told that they would have the same rates which were prevailing over all the steamship lines which come to Halifax. The Government, however, entered into an agreement which, as can be seen from a perusal of it, is limited to the mail steamers, and in which it is specially provided that, in order to get these rates, they must make their terminus at Halifax; that is that all the passengers and all the freight from the steamers which get these favourable terms shall be landed* at Halifax and that no portion shall be brought on by steamer to the port of St. John. That is highly discriminatory against the port of St. John; and it is highly objectionable that a road, which is owned

by the whole .people of Canada, and to which the people of St. John contribute just as much as the people of other portions in the Dominion of equal population should be used in discriminating' against that port.
The suggestion was made that the question should be submitted to the,Board of Railway Commissioners; but the committee will realize at once that, as the Board of Railway Commissioners has no power or authority whatever over the Intercolonial railway, the only way in which that question could be submitted to the board would be by the request of the Government, and the board might then be induced, perhaps, to act as advisers, and to give their opinion in regard to this agreement. But, for reasons which I shall not enter into now, and for which I certainly was in no way responsible, the matter did not come before the board. I at once communicated with the board; and I expected, when the Government submitted the agreement, I would be notified as one of the counsel for the city. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries stated to the House not long ago that he thought it was up to the board of trade to have the matter submitted. However that may be, the question was not submitted; 'but we have also this fact that the Government, through the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, made the statement to the board of trade in St. John, before the entering into operation of the agreement, that, no matter what might be the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the agreement would go into operation, and would remain in force during the time agreed upon. Therefore, you can understand that, even if the Minister of Railways had succeeded in getting the Board of Railway Commissioners to take the matter up and investigate it, the commissioners would be dealing absolutely with a question which would 'be of no practical importance, because the agreement would go into operation in accordance with its terms, 1 hope that, when this question comes up, the Government will decide to divide the mail subsidies' between the two ports, and not to leave it optional to the railway companies as to which poTt they shall use, and that no favouritism will be shown to the Canadian Pacific railway or any other railway company simply because it agrees to use one port or the other.
I hope that will be the case, because it is

only by treating all the companies alike, by having a fixed schedule which will apply both in winter and in summer based somewhat on the mileage of the Intercolonial railway, that full and complete justice can be done to the different sections of Canada that may be interested in the mail service.
Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER: Is it not true that the members of the Board of Trade of St. John decided amongst themselves that the agreement was not discriminatory against St. John, and that that was their reason for not submitting the question to the Board of Railway Commissioners for argument?

All the members of the board with whom I have ever spoken have been of the opinion that the agreement was discriminatory; and only a few days ago there was a resolution passed; a copy of which was published in the newspapers condemning the agreement and expressing the strong hope that the Government would not again enter into a similar arrangement.
Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER: Will they argue the question?

I am arguing it now
before the committee. There is no other tribunal before which I can argue the question. I contend that this agreement is discriminatory. It is making a more favourable arrangement with the Canadian Pacific railway than the tariff in force before the agreement was made, and therefore it is unjust to the port of St. John. Just a question with regard to the boats and the test which was made during the past season. In regard to the Canadian Northern steamers, I congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on the fact that he succeeded in getting the Canadian Northern Royal steamers to come to the port of St. John. He is undoubtedly entitled to all the credit, and the people of St. John were thankful to him for what he did. Many Conservative friends of the minister in St. John can stand pretty bad treatment from the Postmaster General and other members of the Government, and then if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries succeeds only in half righting their wrongs, they are grateful to him and give him credit accordingly. It is not a bad plan to ill-treat the people of St. John and give my hon. friend an opportunity of half-righting the wrong done and of claiming a great deal of credit there-

for. Perhaps the hon. Minister of Railways can tell me what arrangements were made to assist the Canadian Northern in bringing the traffic to St. John. What was the rate *for passengers and freight from St. John to Montreal over the Intercolonial, or were any special rates given?

I have not any information
before me with regard to that. If anything of the kind occurred, it took place prior to my acting for the minister.

Could my hon. friend
ascertain that? When my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries got the Canadian Northern steamships to go to St. John, did he also have the tariff schedule altered in their favour?
As the hon. member knows, if a ticket is sold from a point in Canada to Liverpool via Halifax, the rail rate is not the regular local rate; it is very much lower.

Yes. There was prevailing under the tariff schedule that low rate between Halifax and Montreal and other points so that passengers arriving by steamer at Halifax could have that low rate over the Intercolonial to St. John and over the Canadian Pacific to Montreal. But under this Gutelius-Bosworth agreement, a lower rate was given to the Canadian Pacific in order to induce them to abandon St. John and stop at Halifax. I want to know if a similarly low rate was given to the Canadian Northern, to induce them to take their steamers to St. John for the carriage of passengers and freight to Halifax over the Canadian Pacific railway. My hon. friend the Postmaster General, in speaking of Mr. Gutelius, said that he had proved himself a loyal Canadian, true to the interests of the Intercolonial and against the Canadian Pacific railway. Among other things he said, as found on page 4615 of ' Hansard ':
And Mr. Gutelius stood by the Post Office Department, stood by the interests of this country, and put before us figures which could not be controverted by the Canadian Pacific railway. He fought the battle of the Post Office Department and of the country against the Canadian Pacific railway. When last year a question arose about what road was to transport the ocean mails during the winter season, the Canadian Pacific railway did their best to secure that contract; but Mr. Gutelius fought the battle of the Intercolonial railway and was able to induce the Post Office Department to send the mails by the Intercolonial railway as against the Canadian Pacific railway.
That is for the Halifax mails.
What about the St. John mails?
We do not pay anything at all to the Intercolonial for the carriage of the St. John mails.
Was this fight Mr. Gutelius -made simply to induce the Post Office Department to send the mails from Halifax to Montreal over the Intercolonial railway?
Yes.
Did anybody make any fight to have all the mails landing by the Royal and other steamers at St. John sent over the Canadian Pacific railway to Montreal?
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company did.

Did the Post Office
Department do so?

No; this arrangement
was in respect of the Halifax mails, for the carrying of which the department paid a certain amount. The Intercolonial railway did not get anything for carrying the mails from St. John to Moncton; this was done in the usual course. What I referred to in the statement read by my hon. friend was the question as to who should take the mails from Halifax to Montreal and obtain the amount which the Post Office Department pays for that service.
As I understand it, the Post Office Department was contending that these mails should be carried over the Canadian Pacific railway.
No.

Oh, yes. The minister
says:
Mr. Gutelius fought the battle of the Intercolonial railway and was able to induce the Dost Office Department-
Which means my hon. friend the Postmaster General.
-to send the mails by the Intercolonial railway as against the Canadian Pacific railway.
That gives Mr. Gutelius the credit of in some way inducing the Postmaster General to send the mails by the Intercolonial railway and to refuse to send them by the Canadian Pacific railway.
That refers to Halifax.

The Postmaster General thought that the mails ought to go by way of St. John and the Canadian Pacific and Mr. Gutelius fought the battle and induced him to send them by the Intercolonial railway; is that correct?

What is the use of
splitting hairs in that way? The Canadian Pacific Railway Company contended that under the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement they were entitled to the carriage of the mails from Halifax to Montreal. Mr. Gutelius thought that- this contention was not right, and the matter was discussed between them with the result that Mr. Gutelius succeeded in. getting the mails for the Intercolonial railway from Halifax to Montreal. The Canadian Pacific railway, therefore, did not succeed in getting the mails from Halifax to, Montreal. Is that clear enough?

That is quite clear, but _ what surprises me is that in getting this done Mr. Gutelius is entitled to so much credit because he fought the battles of the Intercolonial railway, and was able to induce the Post Office Department to send the mails by the Intercolonial railway as against the Canadian Pacific railway. Gutelius must be a great fighter if he succeeded in diverting the Postmaster General from his apparently fixed determination to have these mails carried by the Canadian Pacific, railway instead of by the Intercolonial.

This does not apply to ordinary trains; it is a question of special trains from Halifax to Montreal. Let me repeat that the Canadian Pacific railway contended that under the agreement they were entitled to have his special train from their ship's side for the carriage of the mails from Montreal, but Gutelius set forth the view that the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement did not cover the mails and that consequently the Post Office Department should give the preference to the Government railway. That is the fight which Gutelius made. If a department of the Government undertook to give these mails to the Canadian Pacific railway, I should have considered the Post Office Department bound by that undertaking, and that was why the matter was referred to Gutelius, with the result which I have stated This shows that Mr. Gutelius, who hon. gentlemen say was paid out of special

funds supplied by the Canadian Pacific railway; on that occasion, as on many others, strongly fought in favour of the Intercolonial railway and against the Canadian Pacific railway.

I certainly drew from
the language of the hon. minister as reported the conclusion that in some way Mr. Gutelius had fought the battle, to use the Postmaster General's language, of the Intercolonial railway, and was able to induce the department to send the mails by that railway. It appears, however, that he was fighting the Canadian Pacific railway, not the Post Office Department.

The Minister of Railways ought to be able to give us, and I hope he will, a statement of what would have been the amount received by the Intercolonial for the passengers and freight which they carried as stated in this return under the tariff schedule for inward and outward-bound freight in effect before the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement came into effect. It would be in that way only that we could make a comparison.
I would not consider it fair to have a statement showing the local rates.
I did not say that, I said inw'ard and outward.
There is no way in which we can get a rate from St. John except taking the local rate and applying it to the freight carried under the agreement.

My hon. friend talks as if this was the first time that freight and passengers had ever come to Halifax and been transferred over the Intercolonial railway. For years they have had a tariff ' schedule applying to inward and outward freight between points on the Intercolonial railway and Liverpool and other European ports. The tariff arranged under the agreement of Messrs. Bosworth and Gutelius was simply a modification of the tariff schedule giving more favourable terms, but there is an inward and outward freight schedule which my hon. friend will find in his office.
A shipper from St. John would send direct to Liverpool by water, not by rail to Halifax and thence by steamer; therefore it is not likely there would be any special inward and outward rate.

There is. I saw the schedule which was given to me by a shipper in St. John. Every winter more or less freight comes by steamers to Halifax

for St. John and other points on the Intercolonial railway, and there is a special tariff schedule applying to it.
That would be for small quantities.
No, by the ton.
But that would be small in comparison to the very large shipments. Special agreements are made by all railroads, say for trainloads of freight or 500,000 bushels of grain.

I do not think the Intercolonial railway has ever done that, beyond giving a carload rate. You must have uniformity to operate a railway, and particularly a Government railway. There has always been a tariff schedule giving the apportionment of the rates as between the steamship companies and the railway. I would like to have that laid on the table of the House.

In all that has been said on this question there has not been much real information as to the relative merits of these two ports, My hon. friend from St. John states that the fastest trips of the season made anywhere was by the Royal boats from Bristol to St. John. But a decision based on any one particular case is almost sure to be misleading; that is almost a truism.
The statement read by my hon. friend from Halifax is prepared by the Board of Trade, is explicit and conclusive; it is based on official information given out by the Postmaster General, and covers all the winter sailings, forty-three in number, between Liverpool and Halifax, Bristol and St. John, and Liverpool and St. John; and the net result is that the average saving in time in the carriage of mails between Liverpool and Montreal or Bristol and Montreal is by the Halifax route twelve hours and forty-three minutes. That is not one case, but the average of all the voyages.
If we were to assume, which was, however, not the case, that in every one of these passages via St. John the mails were carried from St. John around by Moncton to Montreal, there would have been added in each case 265 miles more than via Canadian Pacific railway St. John to Montreal. That is, the distance from St. John to Montreal via Canadian Pacific railway is 475 miles, and the distance from St. John via Moncton is 740 miles, a difference of 265 miles. If you take the average running
time of the regular limited expresses on the Intercolonial railway, which is thirty-two miles, that will give you eight hours and twenty minutes more time required to go from St. John to Montreal via Moncton than by Canadian Pacific railway direct.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is assuming that the trains are running under the best conditions, with no interruption by storm or anything of that kind.

We are assuming that the trains are running as they have been operated under the present acting Minister of Railways, always on time.
So that if all these mails landed at St. John had been during the past winter sent by the Intercolonial railway via Moncton to Montreal, which they were not, and we deduct eight hours and twenty minutes, which is the ordinary running time which could be saved by sending via Canadian Pacific railway direct, we would still have saved four hours and twenty minutes by sending same via Halifax. That is to say, supposing that all the mails that came to Halifax were sent over the Intercolonial railway to Montreal, and that all that came to St. John were sent over the Canadian Pacific railway to Montreal, then these results of the past winter service would show that, even taking the short cut across the state of Maine, the Halifax route is four hours and twenty minutes shorter; and that time would be considerably increased if we had available, and could calculate on, the number of trips that the mails went from St. John to Montreal via Canadian Pacific railway.

Does my hon. friend
think it fair to take the average of all the steamers when we bear in mind the fact that the four fastest steamers-the two Empresses and the Alsatian and the Calgarian of the Allan line-went to Halifax. Only two fast boats went to St. John, and therefore it is not fair to make such a comparison.
The Calgarian was not on the route at all, and the Alsatian only made a few trips.
It is counted in.

As the Alsatian made
only a very few trips that would affect the average only very slightly. Furthermore, the Royal liners are stated to be as fast, if not faster than the others which he mentions and therefore in the latter case my hon. friend's arguments would rather cut

the other way. The difference in distance 'between Bristol and St. John and Liverpool and St. John is according to the Admiralty chart which I have under my hand only seven miles, making a difference of only half an hour in time at the most.
The hon. member for St. John has talked much of local freight rates and export rates. He mentioned particularly that the rate on lumber between Halifax and St. John is $2.75 per ton although I think that has not much bearing on the question of mail service.
It does seem to be rather hard that the management of the Intercolonial should be publicly condemned because they have had the courage to take advantage of the opportunity of making a business arrangement to increase the traffic of the Intercolonial. If you are operating a railroad or any other business and see an opportunity of increasing your business without any increase of capital expenditure, surely it is wise to take that opportunity by the band. The additional business the Intercolonial railway has secured would not have been obtained if they had not taken advantage of the opportunity when it came along. I have not seen the figures which my hon. friend asks for. I do not know what rates were given on Canadian Northern Northern business from St. John to Montreal, but I venture to say that prior to the time of the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement the Intercolonial had given freight rates much lower that the ones specified in that agreement.
Will the hon. gentleman instance a case?

The rates given the
Canadian Northern on their through business from Chicago to Halifax, at the time the Royal Steamship line was first established, were, I venture to say, considerably lower than the rates in the Gu'telius-Bosworth agreement. I make that statement without knowledge of what these rates were, but I know it would have been impossible for the Intercolonial
5 p.m. to have secured the business in competition with lines out of New York and Portland unless its rates had been lower than in this agreement. The hon. gentleman has figured out that the Intercolonial can haul traffic at six-tenths of a cent per ton mile; that is the actual operating cost for moving a ton of freight, he says. That of course must be an arbitrary figure.
Based on the long experience of the railway authorities.

Well, taking sixtenths of a cent as the actual figure, I can assure my hon. friend that very much lower rates than that have been given by tbe Intercolonial tor ten years back. Such rates were in effect a great many years ago when hon. gentlemen opposite were in control and operating the road. I find no fault with these rates being given. Every one knows that rates must meet conditions if business is to be done. The rates given on steel products from Sydney to Montreal are much lower than six-tenths of a cent per ton mile. These products may be carried at a loss-I do not know about that-but if a low rate were not given they would not be shipped by rail, but largely by water. As I said, the rates that must be made depend upon existing conditions and you cannot make the conditions.
A condition of affairs faced the Intercolonial whereby by giving certain rates, and at no additional expense for rolling stock or on capital account, they could increase the business of the road substantially. I think the management of the Intercolonial are to be commended for getting that 'business. I imagine if my hon. friend has made any mistake in his figures it would not be in favour of the Intercolonial.
It is easy to figure out. Simply multiply six-tenths of a cent by the number of tons.

If my hon. friend has
made an error it would certainly not be against his own argument. I will take his figures as correct, but even then the rate was not so low as had been given on previous occasions at earlier dates. Under the conditions which existed a low rate had to be given in order to secure the business; therefore, it was good business on the part of the management to give a fine rate. I do not think they are at all open to censure for doing that, but rather to be commended.

I think I should not let this matter pass without saying something-I was going to say repeating something, which, to my mind, is of very great importance. There seems to be an impression in the minds of some of the business people of Canada, and this sentiment has been expressed on the floor of the House, that the ocean mail service, instead of having been improved by the contract of last year, was degraded. We are told that we used to pay $600,000 as a subsidy, but we now pay $1,000,000, and that the service is inferior to that which we had

before. I am not surprised at that statement, because it seems to be the opinion of a good many business men . in Canada, and some of the boards of trade. I -would like to explain, and I hope this will be given as wide publicity as possible, because if this kind of thing continues we will have to think very seriously whether we shall continue the Canadian subsidy at all-that we had four steamers on the Canadian mail service before 1913. We now have twelve in summer and eight in winter. For this very great and very marked difference we pay $400,000 in addition to the $600,000 that we- used to pay. An impression has gained ground that our new Canadian service is bad, and I want to dispel that belief if it is at all possible. What are the facts? I admit at once that we were disappointed in one respect. We fully expected that the Alsatian and Calgarian would go into the service much earlier under our 1913 contract than they did. There were strikes and a good many difficulties encountered which prevented them from going into the service late in the year of the contract. We have in consequence suffered to a great extent. But, with the Alsatian and the Calgarian in the service, the Canadian mail service-and I would like these words to be heard by every business man in Canada-is as good as the New York service. Some of the New York steamers are faster than our own steamers, but the distance which the Canadian steamers have to traverse is shorter; consequently, we are able to hold our own with our Now York competitors and send our mails to Liverpool or Bristol as promptly as by way of the New York service, except, perhaps, when the Lusitania and Mauretania happen to carry the mails.
I would like to ask the Postmaster General upon what statistics he bases that statement?
We are sure of that. We have the facts and the data in the department. We have all the data at our fingers' ends.

'Speaking from my private experience, and that of a great many others who correspond regularly with Europe, we have thought that by putting ' via New York ' on our letters we would ensure their getting to their destination sooner and the same thing holds good with reference to letters coming from the other side. I should like to know what the statistics are.

I can tell my hon.
friend a very curious circumstance that occurred repeatedly last year. We had any number of complaints that letters coming to Canada were delayed. We investigated every case and we found that the complaints made to- us about the Canadian service had reference to letters coming via New York to Canada. This fact was shown by the letters enclosed and forwarded to us in support of the complaints made. The blame wae put on the 'Canadian service notwithstanding the fact that the service had been performed by the New York steamers. That the .service was performed by the New York steamers was due to the absence from the Canadian service of the Alsatian and the Calgarian. The British post office practically refused to send any letter mail during last winter by the Canadian boats so that, except in two or three cases, the whole of the letter mail came from England via New York. Yet we were blamed for that. As a matter of fact, most of the complaints that we received came under the supervision of the inspector of the Post Office Department and it was found that some of the letters in regard to which complaint had been made had been sent to Queenstown and that, in consequence of storms or other causes,- the Lusitania, or the Mauretania, could not stop at Queenstown to take on the mails. Consequently, these mails, which had come from London to Queenstown, had to be sent back to London and to wait for .another boat. It .is not surprising that the mails were delayed but they were delayed by the New York service. We had the data of all that, we iare in. a position to substantiate what I say and let me add that we would not have undertaken to pay that $400,000 a year more if we had not known that the Canadian steamers could take care of this service1.
The boards of trade have passed resolutions declaring that this service must continue via New York because they say it is the better one. We know that it is not the better one if we can get our service in proper shape. Last year circumstances were against us; we did not have the Alsatian and the Calgarian, but I ask the boards of trade, now that we are to have the Alsatian and the Calgarian in the service, not to pre judge the question and not to adhere to their conclusion that the Canadian service is no good and that we must send our mail via New York.
While circumstances prevented the Alsa-

tion and Calgarian going into the service as early as we would have liked them to have gone last year, we have this year this most terrible and appalling disaster to the Empress of Ireland which will deprive us of one of the ships engaged in this service. In addition to all the other circumstances connected with this awful accident, of course, Canada is going to suffer in that this ship was one of the twelve in the summer service and one of the eight in the winter service. Our contractors say that this is a case of force majeure and that they cannot replace this ship except by an inferior one. I want this service to be accepted by Canada as a whole and I must tell the committee that we will have to discontinue paying these large sums if the contractors cannot put on a service which can, as far as speed goes, properly replace the Empress of Ireland and we will have to use the New York boats for the service because I do not want this service to again receive the black eye that it received last year when the Corsican and Hesperian were in the service and when the letter mail was sent from the British post office via New York. I shall not go over the whole of the ground that my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) traversed in discussing the question as to the relative claims of the ports of Halifax and St. John.

What are the terms of
the contract as regards the number of years during which it shall remain in force.

It was a contract for twelve months. The question of which should be the winter port for Canadian mails was discussed very fully on a former occasion, and I said what I had to say on the question, so that I hope my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) will not be offended if I do not repeat it now. I stated then that the two ports would have to stand on their own merits, and that the contractors would have to make their own choice. This statement I repeat now, and the two ports will be treated fairly by the Government.
Is the new contract signed?

I understand that the terms of the contract are pretty well arranged. We had to make other arrangements on account of the new ships, and, much to the regret of the Allan Company, I said I would not have this year the Grampian, the Corsican, and the Hesperian.

They have made arrangements to have the Teutonic, which is a very fast ship, come into the service. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself have practically now completed the terms of the contract, but of course provision will have to be made to get a substitute for the Empress of Ireland. The hon. gentleman said that St. John had got the double-cross in our dealings with the Intercolonial railway and the Canadian Pacific railway. I may tell him that we have tried to deal with these matters as best we could, and we have, I think, succeeded, except of course from the point of view of gentlemen who will find fault anyway. As to the mails, we had a special train from Halifax, which the post office paid for, and we had a special train also when the mails came to St. John. We did not discriminate between one port and the other in that respect. But when there was no letter mail for other points ecxept the Maritime provinces, we thought, and I think everybody will agree with me, that it would have been a poor business to pay for a special train to carry parcels and magazines, the latter of which we practically carry for nothing from Liverpool to Vancouver. I think, however, it is worth while to have a special train for letter mail. Whenever there were letter mails on the steamers coming to Halifax, we had a special train from Halifax to Montreal over the Intercolonial, and paid for it, and when the ships came to St. John -I want my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to understand this clearly-there was no question as to sending the letter mail over the Canadian Pacific railway or the Intercolonial railway, because the distance between St. John and Montreal via Moncton, is so much greater than by the Canadian Pacific Railway route that it would be ridiculous to send by any other route than the Canadian Pacific railway. On any occasion when we had a special train from St. John we had it on the Canadian Pacific railway.
How many special trains were there on the Canadian Pacific railway?

There was one every
time there was any mail, two or three times.

I may be wrong, but I
am under the impression that mail very frequently went from St. John by the passenger train some t few hours after the mails landed.

The hon. gentleman is mistaken on that point, and I would like

him and his friends in St. John to understand exactly how the matter stands. If any mail matter went over the Intercolonial it was because there was no letter mail. Mr. Gutelius-this very bad man, who is accused by gentlemen opposite of being a Canadian Pacific railway spy, and accused by gentlemen who do not know what they are talking about
You do not know yourself.

Oh, the member for
Temiscouata has been heard from.

You had better not
mention Mr. Gutelius' name here.
Well, we are speaking about serious business now.
You are off the track.

I want to tell my hon. friend from St. John that the Intercolonial railway without hesitation and without difficulty, exerted themselves and gave us first-class accommodation for parcels and magazines, while the Canadian Pacific railway would not facilitate them for the reason or under the pretense that their train was overloaded. They would not take these mails at St. John unless we paid for a special train. On the other hand, we had the help of Mr. Gutelius in that respect, and he gave us good service and gave it promptly. Evcry-time we wanted him to help the Post Office Department, we found him right there ready to help us. I do not think hon. gentlemen opposite will contend that we should have special trains' to carry magazines and periodicals. At all events I am not prepared to recommend it, because I do not think it would be good business. We have provided in o-ur new arrangement with the railways that when letter mail comes to either Halifax or St. John we will have a special train to carry the letters for important points like Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Winnipeg, etc. We have tried to be fair and we have succeeded, and there is no diouble-oross as my hon. friend from St. John says.

I remember during the early part of the season when one of the steamers was coming in, the people of St. John made inquiry and they were assured that there was a large quantity of first-class mail matter on board.
There was none.
My information is to the contrary.
Oh, your information may be that, but, of course, the Post Office Department knows better.

The Post Office Department made the assertion that there was no first-class mail, but when the steamer arrived it was found there were a good many bags of letters. That was the statement published in the newspapers, and not contradicted.
It was contradicted.

Do I understand that under the new arrangement all letter m'" coming by the mail steamers to St. John will be carried by a special train over the Canadian Pacific railway, and all letter mail coming to Halifax will be carried by special train over the Intercolonial railway?

So far as the Halifax * special trains are concerned, nothing has been decided about that yet, but so far as the St. John end of it is concerned, there is no question that if we have a special train at all we will have a special train over the Canadian Pacific railway. If we engage a special train it is in order to have the mails in Montreal, Toronto, and other points at the earliest possible moment, and that object would be defeated if we chartered a special train and sent the mail around by Moncton.

I want to get at that a little more definitely. I understand the Postmaster General to say that where there is letter mail it will be taken by special train from St. John and Halifax respectively. Will the letter mail coming to St. John be taken by a special train over the Canadian Pacific railway ?
When the British authorities send the mail by St. John that will be done, but it is not going to be done if the British authorities send the bulk of the letter mail matter via New York.

That is not very definite.
Sir WILFRID LAURlER:	The Postmaster General said he would have to send some of the mail via New York on account of the disaster to the Empress of Ireland. I hope he will not have,to do that. I am a great believer in the 'Canadian route; and I believe that, even taking into account this great disaster, time will show that the route over the St. Lawrence is safer than any other, and that it will become in course of time the most popular of all. Mail steamers from Canadian ports
RarisED bditooh

have the advantage of distance, although mail steamers from New York have the advantage of speed. It cannot Ibe expected that the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company will be able this summer to replace the Empress of Ireland with a boat of equal capacity; but, knowing their spirit of enterprise, we are sure they'will give as good a boat as it is possible to supply. Therefore, for my part, I have no doubt at all that the St. Lawrence route will not long suffer from the bad impression created by the accident. I have great confidence that the investigation will show that the disaster was not due at all to the locality of the St. Lawrence, and that the same thing might have happened under similar circumstances in mid-ocean. The impression, however, prevails, which has been voiced by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), that there is an advantage in sending mails via New York. If two steamers happen to leave on the same day, one via New York and one via Montreal,
I do not think there is any advantage via New York. The only advantage in routing via New York at the present time is that there is a sailing every day from New York, whereas there are only two sailings a week from Canada. Otherwise I am satisfied that the St. Lawrence route is equal to the New York route and that in course of time it will become the more popular one.
We have three sailings a week in summer: Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I suppose the case
to which my hon. friend the Postmaster _ General alludes is one in which the ruleB of the International Postal Union would have some effect, and I believe he had that in mind when he spoke of the necessity of sending the mails via New York.
What are those rules?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will explain them in a moment. The application of the rules would lie in this, that, if a steamer from Great Britain to New York were so much faster than the one that could be put on in place of the Empress of Ireland that the mails could be landed here more quickly via New York than via the substituted steamer, the British post office would have the right under the rules of the International Postal Union to route the mails via New York.

So far as the whole question is concerned, I would like to add just a few words. There is a very natural rivalry between the ports of Halifax and St. John; and that rivalry, of course, leads the inhabitants of each city to be very zealous and diligent to see that the interest of their port are not neglected. The proposal which the Government brought down and which was acted upon last year left the selection to the steamship companies. We are accused by our opponents in 'St. John of having interfered on behalf of Halifax. We are accused by our opponents in Halifax, of having interfered on behalf of St. John. As a matter of fact, we did not interfere on behalf of one port or the other, but left the matter to be determined by the steamship companies themselves. There was a declaration by the Canadian Northern in the first instance that their boats were going to Halifax. There was also a declaration by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in the first instance that all their boats were going to St. John. As a matter of fact, they saw fit to change their arrangements; but in the end, if I remember aright four steamers made their terminus at St. John and four made their terminus at Halifax.
As far as the agreement between the Intercolonial railway and the Canadian Pacific railway in respect of the carrying of freight and passengers between Halifax and St. John is concerned, in regard to through export traffic and the traffic to western Canada, it was necessarily felt by the people of Halifax that they should not be absolutely excluded from all transportation benefits accruing to the whole country from the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. Therefore, it was a proper thing that fair arrangements should be made between the Intercolonial and the Canadian Pacific railway in respect to the new situation thus brought about. I am thoroughly convinced, so far as one who is not an expert in these matters can be, that the arrangement did not discriminate against either Halifax or St. John. There is no reason why Mr. Gutelius, or any one else connected with the Intercolonial, should desire to discriminate against one port or the other. Persons having the management of the Government railway system would naturally desire an agreement which would not be a losing proposition to the Intercolonial; and

I believe the agreement was not a losing one, but was a reasonable and a paying one in view of the large amount of traffic which was acquired. My hon. friend the member for the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) thinks that the subsidy should be divided. My hon. friend and colleague from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) considers that a contract should be entered into by which these steamships should sail altogether from Halifax for the purpose of mail-carrying. We have thought better to leave the matter open, as it was left open last year, and it will remain for the steamship companies under these circumstances to make their arrangements for sailing. I have not any doubt that the matter will be worked out by the steamship companies in a fair way.
I agree entirely with what my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has said as to the necessity of maintaining the Canadian route in every possible way. It was unfortunate last year that the construction of the Alsatian and the Calgarian was delayed. It is unfortunate this year that we have lost the steamship Empress of Ireland. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company will no doubt do everything that their great resources will permit and that their great enterprise will suggest, to replace that steamer by at least an equally good steamer in the near future. It may be necessary, for some time during the summer before that can be accomplished, that a slower steamer should be put on; but we have every confidence indeed that the loss in that regard will be replaced by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at the earliest practicable moment.

It is evident that under the present Administration we are condemned to drink very often the cup of humiliation as regards our relations with the mother country. Last year, when my hon. friend the Postmaster General laid on the table of the House a new contract which had been made between the Government and the steamship companies, he laid it with a glorious gesture and declared that this was another step forward in the closer connection between Canada and the mother country; that it was a step which would bring us nearer to the motherland. I said to myself at the time that he was not a very high stepper from the obscure names he gave the House when he mentioned the second-class. type of ships which were to bring nearer and sooner to the shores of the motherland the Canadian mails. Events have proved that my apprehensions were 319 J
true. We were paying, in round figures', about $600,000 to steamship companies, and we never heard at the time of the disgust, shall I say, of the people in England and in Canada when they spoke of the handling of the transatlantic mails. This morning I put on the Order Paper the following question, which illustrates the case very plainly:
Has the Postmaster General read the following letter which appeared in the London Times of the 22nd May, 1914:
To the Editor of the Times.
Sir,-'The mail service hetween Canada and Great Britain is a disgrace to both governments.' I am ready to endorse this statement, which is quoted from a letter of Mr. C. N. Armstrong in the Times of May 13.
I am managing director for a firm of book publishers in Toronto. We buy paper, printing, binding, etc., from Great Britain to the amount of $30,000 to $50,000 annually. The average time it takes to receive a reply from a correspondent here by return post is about three weeks. There is no reasonable regularity; sometimes it is a month, and again, only 15 days. Is not such a mail service a stupid and wholly unnecessary handicap on business between these two parts of the empire? Would it not pay the people of both Great Britain and Canada to do something to improve the service?
Sincerely yours,
Robert Glasgow.
Edinburgh.
As I stated a moment ago, in 1911, when the late Government was in power, we were paying $600,000, in round figures, as mail subsidies. We are now paying $1,000,000 for what has been described by Mr. C. N. Armstrong, a friend of the Government, by Mr. Robert Glasgow, in the London Times, and by many people in Canada, as a disgrace and as a stupid mail service. Last year, when my hon. friend laid the contract on the table of the House, we were told that this great service would help to bind us more closely to the mother land. As I said a moment ago, we have drunk the draught of humiliation many times since the new Administration came into office. I surely do not rejoice in my country's misfortune, but I am bound to say that while we had the right hon. leader of the Opposition as Prime Minister of this country, although he was a good target for the jingoes, he always stood for sane imperialism; we had a splendid mail service between the Dominion and the mother country, and we never had such 'Complaints as are made in the columns of the Times, where this service is described as disgraceful and stupid. Yes, we are being humiliated by the jingoes who took office in 1911. The Hindus are kept literally at bay in the harbour of Vancouver, for the sake of empire of
Robert Glasgow says that.

I would rather accept the view of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, who takes a broad view of this question, than that of the hon. member for Rouville, who has dragged into the discussion of this mail contract service the Hindus and a lot of other extraneous references. The hon. member for Rouville says that we have a rotten service.
The Times says that.
The Times does not say that.
It is said to be a disgrace. ,	[DOT]

I have always been
anxious to know why we paid the extra' $400,000.

Because we had only four ships in the service before 1913, with one trip a week; whereas now we have in the summer twelve ships, with three trips a week: one on Tuesday, one on Thursday, and one on Saturday; and during the winter we have eight ships, with two sai'ings a week: one on Wednesday and one on Saturday. This explains the difference of $400,000.

As I understand, the
reason for the mail subsidies is to get the mails to their destination; and if, as a matter of fact, the mails do not reach their destination any more quickly or any more certainly when we are paying the $400,000 than they did before we paid that, it seems as if we are paying the money for nothing.

They reach their destination as quickly as by a foreign port, and in greater quantities. We used before 1913 to pay to the Government of the United States a very large sum which, under the Postal Union laws, we had to pay to a foreign government for taking care of our mails at their ports. Both these amounts will be saved now by Canada, to be used to pay the increase in the cost of the Canadian mail service. With the boats we now have, including the Alsatian and the Calgarian, we are sure that the mails will reach England as quickly as by New York. If we were not sure of that we would not pay the $400,000 additional. It is unfortunate that last year there were delays in placing the Alsatian and the Calgarian on the route, so that inferior steamers had to be used part of the time; but they are now in the service, and we shall have a very fast service. The final success of this matter will be our answer
to the gentlemen who are now criticising the arrangements.

Lest we forget, as my hon. friend attributed to me the words of one of his friends in England, Mr. C. N. Armstrong, a Unionist candidate, I will again read his letter, published in the London Times, the chief organ of imperialism on the other side:
TO the Editor of the Times.
' sir.-Tire mail service between Canada and Great Britain is a disgrace, to both Governments.' I am ready to endorse this statement, which is quoted from, a letter of Mr. C. N. Armstrong in the Times of May 13.
I am managing director for a firm of book publishers in Toronto. We buy paper, printing, binding, etc., from Great Britain to the amount of $30,000 to $50,000 annually. The average time it takes to receive a reply from a correspondent here by return post is about three weeks. There is no reasonable regularity ; sometimes it is a month, and again, only fifteen days. Is not such a mail service a stupid and wholly unnecessary handicap on business between these two parts of the empire? Would it not pay the people of both Great Britain and Canada to do something to improve the service?
Sincerely yours,
Robert Glasgow.
Edinburgh.
Mr. Glasgow quotes from Mr. Armstrong, and I simply .quote the letter. Last year, when the new contract was laid on the table of the House, my hon. friend stated that this would bring us closer to the motherland; it was a step forward, to bind us closer to the mother country. We now find from people in the motherland itself, that this contract is a disgrace and that this is a stupid and wholly unnecessary handicap.

I could understand our paying $400,000 a year more if we were getting a quicker and better service; but I understood from the Postmaster General that we were not expecting to get either a quicker or a better service than we were getting before.

Why, certainly we
are.

It was to go by Canadian vessels, but it was going to be, as he said, as quick by Canadian vessels as it had been by United States vessels. He did not profess that it would be any quicker. The House and the country should understand that this $400,000 is being paid for the benefit of the steamship companies and not for the benefit of the Canadian people, or that part of the Canadian people who have to carry on correspondence with Great Britain. But the evidence is that while my

hon. friend expected to get his mails carried as quickly and as surely by the payment of $400,000 as he had been getting them carried without that payment, he is not getting the mails carried either as quickly or as certainly as before. The minister should explain this or reconsider the situation. This is a rich country and we wish our steamship companies well; but we have had evidence placed before this House repeatedly during this session as to the holdup practised by these very steamship lines. I understand that the matter was brought to the attention of the Government within the last week by an important section of the Canadian community. It is in order that there should be a more definite and lucid explanation than any that has been given why that $400,000 should be paid.
Mr. GEO. E. FOSTER: I think my hon. friend has, not designedly, got in wrong on this question. I do not see how he comes to this conclusion. He says we pay $400,000 more than we formerly paid and have no better service than before.
I understand not as good.

Let us try it out. Under the old service we had one mail per week in summer and one mail per week in winter. Now we have three mails out of Canada every week in summer and two mails out of Canada every week in winter. Under the former state of things the great majority of our letters went via New York. Under the present state of things the great majority of our letters go by Canada. I think these two considerations themselves are fairly indicative of the effect of the change in the. contract. But we are also doing better in the class of vessels. Contrast in speed and quality the vessels of four years ago with the vessels of to-day. I had the advantage of coming over in one of the latest boats, the Alsatian. It is as well appointed a boat as there is on the Atlantic service and made a trial speed of over twenty knots. The Calgarian is equally good, if not better. Four years ago we had no vessel that could compare with them, and if it had not been for the accident which we all deplore, we would have had four vessels with a speed of over eighteen knots, and these two new Allan liners with a. speed of nineteen or twenty knots-easily nineteen knots on a voyage from land to land. Our fleet of vessels carrying our letters, papers and parcels is infinitely better than it was four years ago. Do we or do we not want to carry

Canada's mail matter through our own ports and have the proceeds from the carrying of this mail matter come into our own revenue ? Is it not a matter of pride as well as a matter of national importance that instead of paying foreign countries for carrying our mail we should carry it ourselves, and gradually come to the time when we shall have a service the equal of any on the Atlantic. I agree with what my right hon. friend has said. We have the advantage in point of distance as between port and port, and with eighteen and nineteen-knot boats we can put the mail into the interior parts of Canada and into the interior parts of the United States quicker than it can be done via New York. I think that is a fair way of looking at it, and that it gives us a better view of our improved mail service than was given by my hon. friend.
Just a word or two about the remarks of my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). Mr. C. N. Armstrong is one man, but there are 45,000,000 people in Great Britain, and 8,000,000 people in this country, and it is a very dangerous thing to stand up in Parliament and give a black eye to a service because one man out of forty or fifty million people writes to The Times, for some reason or other, and says that the mp.il time between Great Britain and this country runs anywhere from between fifteen days to a month. If five thousand Armstrongs made that statement, I would still say that it was erroneous. There are very few times when it takes the mail fifteen days to get across and there never is a time when it takes a whole month. I am very sensitive as to the impression that is caused by a member of Parliament making statements on an important matter of this kind-I am not administering any reproof to my hon. friend,
I do not propose to do that-which have a tendency to degrade and disparage our own service in the eyes of both our own ' people and those abroad, because it goes out that The Times newspaper has declared that this service is a disgrace.

On several occasions
last winter I brought letters to the attention of my hon. friend from his own electors . complaining of the service.

Did my hon. friend ever
know a period in his lifetime, or does he ever expect to know a period in his lifetime, which I hope will be long, when somebody did not write a letter to somebody

else saying that some particular thing was not being done as it should be done? Long dates of passage are given out when they ought not to be given out. It may be that the delay takes place between the time that the letter was written and the time it gets into the post office and into the fast steamer which takes it to the other side.

I appreciate the remarks which have been made toy my hon. friend in such good spirit. I read The Times regularly, and if I can get a copy in the reading room for the month of May I will show my hon. friend not later than this evening, column after column reflecting the opinion of this writer to The Times.

Investigations have
been made, and in most of the cases, if not all, we found that the delays complained of were in the case of letters going via New York. I am sure of that

The Postmaster General has stated that most of the letters coming this way come via New York instead of in Canadian ships. Would the Minister of Trade and Commerce kindly explain why the British Government takes that course?

It is very easily
understood. Both the British Government and this Government are bound by the laws and regulations of the International Postal Union to put letter mail on the ship which will carry it to its destination in the quickest way. The British Government claims that it is bound by those laws, and so it is. There is no disposition on the part of the British Post Office to hurt Canada. Then they must be complaining of the Canadian service in regard to letters which they themselves have marked to go via New York.

My hon. friend does not catch the point. Numerous complaints were made in regard to delay in the receipt of letters. We investigated every case and found that most of the complaints were in regard to letters coming via New York.
Those complaints were made to the minister's office by private persons. The cases investigated were not the ones complained of by the correspondents of the Times.

I do not read the
Times.
