The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

This is an important matter, and one that, I think, we ought to thresh out until we get to a conclusion. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said he thought I was in wrong in my statement of the case. On the other hand, I think that, judging him by his statement of the case, he is decidedly in wrong. The question that I asked, and which, I think, is the question that we are entitled to be satisfied upon, is this: Has the mail service between Canada and Great Britain been improved since the granting of $400,000 additional subsidy, as compared with what it was before that subsidy was granted? That question is answered by the knowledge of how long it takes a letter to get to England from Canada, and with what little delay it takes a letter to get from England to Canada. It is not answered with information as to what vessel carries the letter or by what route it is carried. I am quite willing to admit that, if, by the vote of $400,000 additional subsidy, we get our letters carried to Great Britain quicker, or business letters from Great Britain are carried to Canada quicker than they were before, proportionate to the amount of extra money paid, there might be some justification for the extra payment. But, if we are not getting our letters carried more quickly than and with less delay than we were before, then, from the standpoint of the mail service, there is no value received for this amount of money that is being paid. My hon. friend has said that there are so many vessels sailing from Canada each week now as compared with the number that we had before. I presume that he means the number that are carrying mail now as compared with those that were carrying mail before. I think that, as a matter of fact, with the

exception of the two new vessels, we have exactly the same vessels and the same number of sailings that we had two years ago. There is no difference in the number of sailings or in the class of vessels except with respect to the two additional and superior vessels which have been put on the Canadian route.
If it is for the purpose of getting better vessel accommodation for freight and passengers on the Canadian route, then I can understand why this money is being paid; but I cannot understand why money should be paid, presumably to improve the mail communication, when, on all the evidence which has been placed before us to-day, there has been no improvement in the mail communication. As to the value to the country of having two very fine steamers in addition to the fleet already plying between Great Britain and Canada in the service, I am not prepared to say that under certain circumstances there might not be an advantage that might compensate for the extra payment that has been made. But the point I want to bring out is that, as far as freight is concerned, we are not'getting any advantage whatever from that extra payment. As a matter of fact, the papers report that within the last few days a deputation of the millers of Canada called upon the Government and complained that their trade was being injured, that they were being driven out of the European market with their product, by reason of the rates that the vessels charge on flour from Canada to British and European ports. If there is merit in their contention, and there is no doubt whatever that there is merit to the extent that ocean rates have been abnormal during the past year or two, then I say it is evident that as far as the freight traffic is concerned, we have paid this $400,000 a year and we have got nothing for it. I am not so sure that we have not got worse than nothing because there is a good deal to be said in favour of the argument that the subsidies that we pay to certain lines of steamers enables them to keep away from the ports that they sail from steamers that are not subsidized. The very money that we are paying these vessels enables them to establish a monopoly which again enables them to charge a rate of freight which, though it is decidedly profitable to themselves, drives Canadian traffic to United States ports. This is a sufficiently serious eon-

sideration, it appears to me, to warrant more and better reasons than have been given to the public for the vote of this additional subsidy.
To revert to the postal question, I can appreciate the desirability of improving mail communication between, Canada and Great Britain; I can appreciate the propriety of paying out Canadian money for the purpose of providing Canadian facilities that will give that improved communication; but I cannot appreciate the purpose of giving Canadian money if the service is not improved. It just means a hand-out from the Government of Canada with the authority of Parliament to certain steamship companies. Such a vote, without better reasons being given for it, is absolutely unwarranted. It may be desirable that we should have magnificent steamers plying between Canada and Great Britain; it may be that it is worth paying for; but Canada is not- getting any return in the way of a mail or freight service for, this $400,000 a year that is being paid in addition to what was paid formerly.

The hon. gentleman
overlooks one important feature of this matter, namely, that when our mails go iby New York we pay for them in Canadian money to foreign vessels. When these same mails are taken to Great Britain through Canadian ports, we also pay, but we pay to Canadian ships employing Canadian labour. Our estimate of what we would have been obliged to pay to the United States Government this year if we had not taken care of our own mails vi>a Canadian ports, would be, speaking from memory, in the vicinity of $350,000. Instead of paying that to the United States Government, we paid it and a little more, to Canadian ships coming to Canadian ports, and my hon. friend must not forget that, which to me is a very important consideration. The hon. gentleman says we are paying $400,000 more and receiving nothing in return. If we do pay that amount, and 'because of paying it we pay less than we otherwise would pay to the United States Government, we are getting some consideration.
I appreciate that.

There is only the
usual service now that we have had for years?
It is increasing enormously.
It is only three times a week?
Yes, that is our present contract; but it was only once a week before.

The statement made by the Postmaster General is perfectly logical if all the facts correspond; but we have already heard in the House that notwithstanding this payment of $400,000 and the additional 'service from Canadian ports, we still receive 'and send a considerable portion of our mail via New York. The fact that we do send by preference part of our mail through New York, and that by preference part of our mail comes from Great Britain by way of New York, is absolute evidence that we are not getting a service on the direct route equal to the service iby way of New York. If we were getting better service for the increased amount of money well and good, but we are not.

On the motion of the Hon. George E. Foster, that the committee rise and report progress:

Before the committee rises, I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the question of improving the transportation system, so as to facilitate the shipment of the products of the fisheries of the Atlantic, particularly in southwestern Nova Scotia. Mr. GEORGE E. FOSTER: In reference to the representations which were made to me, and to which my hon. friend (Mr. McCurdy) has alluded, I may state that I received a deputation from the southern part of the coast of Nova Scotia, which was accompanied by my hon. friend, and these gentlemen went very carefully into this matter with respect to the product and the progress of the fisheries on that part of the Nova Scotia coast, chiefly extending from Lunenburg to Yarmouth, or in that section. They represented that they had had some difficulty in getting these fresh fish products in particular quickly and in good condition into the Boston market, because the Yarmouth line of boats running

I trust that, when the minister works out a scheme, he will not forget that the main winter fishing in Nova Scotia is in the eastern part of the province, and that the headquarters of our fishing industry centres about 'Canso and vicinity. The best fishing grounds on the Atlantic coast of Canada are Tight off Canso, which juts out into the sea pretty close to what is known as the banks where the haddock ,and cod are caught. If there is to be a fast fish steamboat line between any point in Canada and the United States market, it ought to start from some point near Canso. I suppose it would be quite possible to connect Shelburne and the district around that point with Yarmouth and make the Yarmouth service accommodate Shelburne, but for eastern Nova Scotia the case is very different. I pointed out to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in a recent discussion-and 1 do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was present at the time-that we could develop a very large trade in eastern Nova Scotia if we had the advantage of steamship communication with the Boston market, and that it would be of enormous advantage to our fishermen. The fact that the price of fresh fish has gone up at Yarmouth since the duty was taken off last year in the United States is an illustration of what might happen in eastern Nova Scotia. The fishermen at Yarmouth are now getting, I am told, nearly 50 per cent more for

their fish than they were getting when the duty was exacted in the United States-. Therefore I trust that, if any scheme is entertained by the Government to assist this project, they will keep in mind that the place where it can be developed to a greater extent than any other pl-ace on the coast is in the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia. I regret very much that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who, I know, is willing to assist in developing our trade in any direction he can, has not been able to work out any scheme this year. I trust, however, he will keep the matter in view, as I can assure him it is of the greatest importance to the fishing industry. I do not believe there is .any other trade that has the same possibilities at the present time; and a liberal subsidy, that would establish a line of bo-ats to carry the fish to Boston and New York market and deliver it there ingood condition, would be of great advantage to the fishing industry on that coast.

That this House doth agree to the second and third amendments made by the Senate to the Bill No. 147, an Act to amend the Post Office Act, but that they disagree to the first of their amendments for the following reasons :
Because the said amendment is not sufficiently explicit in regard to the terms and conditions on which mailable matter shall in each case be permitted to pass by post, or as to the powers of the Postmaster General in regard thereto.
And that a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their Honours therewith.
He said: The merits of the question do not come up at this time. We are obliged to send the Bill back to the Senate, and if any amendment such as we now suggest is to be put in, it will have to be put in by the Senate. With reference to the other

two amendments, we simply notify them that they are agreed to by this House.
I understood this morning that my hon. friend would accept the amendment with a rider attached to it. I have no doubt that under the circumstances the matter may be arranged by conference.
Am I to understand that nothing is settled as regards the amendment?
Nothing.
The Bill will come back to the House?

Yes. The Senate has made an amendment. With a view to agreeing as much as. possible with the views of the president of the Canadian Press Association, we have consented further to amend the amendment of the Senate. According to the rules of the House, however, we cannot now add to the Senate amendment our consequential amendment; therefore the Bill is to go back to the Senate and will then come back to the House for our concurrence, if we do concur.
Under those conditions, I shall defer any remarks I have to make until the Bill comes back.
Motion agreed to.
On the motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) for Committee of Supply:

I purpose moving an amendment to the motion of my hon. friend, as follows:
That all the words of the motion after the word ' that ' be struck out and the following inserted in lieu thereof:
This House regrets that since the present Government came into power there has been an apparently systematic and determined effort to defeat or delay the accomplishment of the great national objects for which the Transcontinental railway was undertaken, of carrying traffic at a low cost between the East and the West, and to secure to the utmost extent possible the transportation of Canadian products and merchandise through Canadian channels and Canadian seaports both in summer and winter, such efforts being evidenced-
(a)	by reducing the standard of construction ;
(b)	by so doing without the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company,

and thus giving the company a reason for refusing or delaying the operation of the eastern division, and for the carrying or its traffic to United States winter ports;
(c)	by delaying the construction of terminal accommodations, at Quebec and Maritime province ports, and also by great and unnecessary delay in the making of provision for suitable connections therewith to be used by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company;
(d)	by neglecting to arrange as provided by statute for the operation by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company of sections of the Transcontinental railway a'ready completed, which, if it had been so arranged for, would have already brought about considerable development of traffic in the districts served by the sections so operated.
I do not intend at this period of the session to debate this at length nor do I think it would be necessary to do so for 'the reason, that all the facts upon which this amendment is based have 'been pretty well presented to the House in the various discussions which have taken place.
With regard to the first section of the amendment, that the standard of the road has been reduced, I think there can be no question, because it has been proved to the entire satisfaction of the House that in a large number of eases the grade has been increased beyond the .4 per cent as againts eastbound traffic and as against .6 per cent as against westbound traffic. There can be no gain-saying that fact. The proof of it will be found in the references made by the hon. member for South Renfrew, which will be found in ' Hansard ' at page 2109, and subsequent pages. There have been a great many instances in which the grades have been increased. I think no one will deny that the lowering of the standard in that respect tends, as my amendment says, to interfere with the national idea of having a great transcontinental road built to the highest standard, which will carry the products of our country from ocean to ocean at the lowest possible cost. That was the idea which was put forward when the Transcontinental was first inaugurated and that was the ideal which the late Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company always kept before them. It does seem an extraordinary thing that the Government should have consented to the degrading of the Transcontinental railway in that particular. It seems most unfortunate that, after the road was nearly completed-after the larger part of the expense of its construction had been, incurred, the Govern-

ment, through its commissioner, Major Leonard, should have set about to reduce the standard by, as I have said, raising the grades and also in some cases substituting wooden structures instead of steel as the contract provides for. It is important to bear in mind that in order to ensure entire satisfaction by the Grand Trunk Pacific with the standard of construction, it was provided that their chief engineer should approve of the plans and specifications for the eastern division of the road, and those plans and specifications provide for the grade which I have spoken of, not exceeding four-tenths of one per cent as against eastbound traffic and six-tenths of one per cent as against westbound traffic. There were a few instances where it was not practicable to obtain those grades and by mutual consent pusher grades were provided for; but taking the whole road from the Atlantic to the Pacific, both that portion which was to be constructed by the Government and that portion which was to be constructed by the company, the plans and specifications provided for a railroad to be built to the highest standard.
The amendment also declares that these changes-this increase in the grade, this lowering of the standard-were made without the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and I would call attention to a letter from Mr. Chamberlin, the president of the .Grand Trunk Pacific to Major Leonard, the chairman of the commission, as follows:
July 18, 1912.
Major R. W. Leonard,
Chairman, Transcontinental Commission, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-I learn from our engineers that the standard of work on that portion of the Transcontinental railway between Lake Superior Junction and Cochrane, which was at the outset adopted and has so far been complied with, is being departed from, and that instead of four-tenths grade and permanent structures, you have authorized grades up to one per cent and the erection of temporary wooden structures. In regard to this I would call attention to clause 7 of this agreement of the 29th July, 1903, which provides that the work of construction of the eastern division shall be done according to the specifications approved by the company and shall be subject to the joint supervision, inspection and acceptance of our chief engineer and the chief engineer of the commission. I beg to say if this work is done in accordance with what I understand to be your recent instructions, it will not he in compliance with the agreement nor satisfactory to this company and cannot be accepted.
(Sgd) E. J. Chamberlin.
There is a distinct statement by the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company calling attention to this departure from the grade and accepted plans and specifications and notifying the commissioner that this change will not be. approved of and that the work cannot be accepted. All the way along on the eastern division, both west of Cochrane and east of Cochrane, these changes were made, and made just as if the Grand Trunk Pacific-had nothing in the world to do with agreeing or not agreeing -with the standard to which the road was to be constructed. Apparently the Government, through their commissioner, Major Leonard, ignored the provisions of the agreement and proceeded with the work entirely independently of the consent of the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I think that nobody will question the fact that this was a most dangerous and unjustifiable proceeding on the part of the Government, because the result is that if the road is constructed to a standard to which the Grand Trunk Pacific has not agreed-if the agreement of July, 1903 is departed from by the Government, it places the Grand Trunk Pacific in the position of being able to insist upon terms upon which they will give consent to take over the portion of the road so altered and so degraded in its character.
I come to the next part of the amendment, which refers to the extraordinary delay which has taken place in the providing of terminals for the Grand Trunk Pacific at the city of Quebec. I am not as familiar with the condition of affairs there as other hon. gentlemen, but the admission cf my hon. friend the Postmaster General is abundant authority for the statement alleged in this amendment that there has been inexcusable delay. What are the facts? As long ago as 1910 or 1911, three or four years ago, plans were prepared; a scheme of improvement at Quebec was laid out providing for yard room, workshops, wharfs, a grain elevator, the location for an immigration shed, a station,-everything was so arranged that the work might be proceeded with without delay. Those plans weTe approved of by the Grand Trunk Pacific authorities. I know that on one occasion when I met the Grand Trunk Pacific authorities in the city of Quebec they expressed their delight at the layout of the proposed improvements. It was expected that the contracts would be let almost immediately and the work proceeded with. In the meantime, I may say that

the work of getting into the heart of the city of Quebec was proceeded with by building a track. from near the point of junction with the Quebec bridge which gradually got down to the city level and entered the station at Champlain market. But, Sir, this Government has been in office since the fall of 1911, pretty nearly three years, and scarcely a thing has been done towards providing the necessary terminals in connection with the Transcontinental at Quebec. The Postmaster General admitted that there has been too much delay, but who is responsible for that? It is the Government and its officials, and whether it is Major Leonard or anybody else that has been the direct factor in bringing about the delay it is this Government and this Government alone that is responsible to the people of this country for the delay which has taken place. I think it is most unfortunate that .when the Grand Trunk Pacific is completed this fall-as it is said it will be-there will be no terminal provisions at Quebec for accommodating the traffic which will come over the Grand Trunk Pacific-no suitable wharfs close to the railway, no grain elevator, no workshops, no yard room, practically nothing whatever provided. Anybody who knows anything about railroading knows how essential it is that all these terminal facilities should be ready when the railway is 9 p.m. opened for traffic. I shall leave the matter of the terminals at Quebec to be dealt with by those who are more familiar with the subject, but I may say that the very statement of the Postmaster General, if we had no other evidence as we have in abundance, would be sufficient to condemn this Government for. the delay which has taken place in connection with the terminals at the port of Quebec. v
Let us look at the city of St. John. When the Transcontinental was planned it never was expected that its terminus, so far as its Transcontinental business was concerned, would be at the city of Moncton. Moncton was only to be the point of junction with the Intercolonial to connect with the great cities of the Maritime provinces. It was expected that connection would be made with the city of St. John, either by the Intercolonial railway or a shorter route, and also connection with the city of Halifax. What is being done in the city of Halifax to interest the Grand Trunk Pacific in carrying traffic to that port I do not 
know, but so far as the port of St. John is concerned I assert that there has been the most criminal negligence which it is possible to imagine. As long ago as 1910 the Grand Trunk Pacific, through Mr. Hays, its chief executive officer, and with the approval of their engineer and other high officials, came to the conclusion that St. John should be one of the termini of their system. They came to St. John and had surveys made and elaborate plans prepared showing their yard room, the location of their roundhouses and of the station and grain elevator, and indeed of all the equipment which properly belongs to the terminals of a great transcontinental system. They purchased some forty or fifty acres of land at the head of the harbour-at Courtenay bay. They had their plans prepared and intended to proceed as rapidly as possible with the improvements, but from that day to this not a step has been taken. No work of any kind or description has been done at St. John towards providing yard room, roundhouse, or in fact in any direction along the lines which were under contemplation when this Government came into office. Prior to the commencement of the development of Courtenay bay I, as Minister of Public Works, conferred with Mr. Hays and Mr. Biggar the solicitor of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and we came to an arrangement under which the Grand Trunk Pacific agreed that the' first two piers immediately after being constructed in Courtenay bay should be leased by the Grand Trunk Pacific upon a rental basis, just as is being done in connection with the Transcontinental railway; in other words, that tiiese piers should be treated as part of the Transcontinental system. A draft of the agreement was prepared by the solicitor of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and when we went out of office that agreement was left on file and I presume is to be found to-day in the office of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. That agreement provided for the use of the wharfs by other railway companies, and the very reasonable stipulation was made that the rental should be divided amongst the companies using the wharfs. From the time this Government came into office, nearly three years ago, nothing has been done towards providing terminal facilities at St. John; no yard room, no roundhouse, no grain elevator, no work of any kind has been done in connection with providing terminals, and to-day by the declaration which the Government has made the Grand Trunk Pacific do not know and cannot

know whether they are to create terminals at St. John or not. Last summer when the people of St. John had the pleasure of a visit from the Minister of Public Works he made the statement publicly at a meeting of the members of the board of trade, and his statement was corroborated by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that the Government did not approve of a railway company having control of wharfs, and they both expressed the opinion that the Government should build terminals and have control of the wharfs, giving all railway companies access to them.
With this policy being announced by the Government, of course, the Grand Trunk Pacific cannot proceed to make any improvements. It is the duty of the Government, and it has been their duty for the past three years, to take hold of this land that the Grand Trunk Pacific have acquired for the purpose of creating these terminals. While (by reason of the inexcusable delay that has taken place they cannot be ready when the Grand Trunk Pacific is open for traffic, while they cannot be ready until two or three years after the Grand Trunk Pacific is opened, they can get to work and have them ready as soon as they reasonably can and make up for the three years which have been lost in connection with this most important work. By reasonof the public statements which have been made by the ministers, and by reason of the fact that during all the time that this Government have been in office, not only has there been uncertainty as to the position of the Grand Trunk Pacific in connection with the operation of the eastern division of the Transcontinental railway and in connection with the terminals at the Maritime Provinces ports, most valuable time which can never be recovered has been lost and lost to the very great detriment of the people of this country.
You, Mr. Speaker, know perfectly well that when the Grand Trunk Pacific railway is opened, as it will be this fall, if there are not suitable terminals at the St. Lawrence and Maritime Province ports, if there is not ample grain elevator accommodation or ample yard room for the storage of cars the Grand Trunk Pacific will necessarily and naturally carry their traffic to the city of Portland in the state of Maine. Is it that hon. gentlemen opposite are desirous that that shall take place, is it that they are desirous that they may Ibe able to point from the public platform to the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific, which was constructed at the public expense as a great national
highway that was to carry the traffic through Canadian channels, has failed in its object? Is that their desire? They have been apparently lacking in doing anything to provide proper facilities to enable the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry traffic through Canadian ports. If that had been their object tan. gentlemen opposite could not have done .anything which would be more likely to bring about that result than to pursue the policy of inaction, inactivity and neglect which has characterized their course during the past three years.
I want to pass on to another part of the amendment. I come to that portion of it which refers to the fact that this Government has not entered into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate the completed sections of that road. It will he borne in mind that the Act of 1904 contemplated that these various sections would be completed from time to time pending the completion of the whole line, and this Parliament, in the year 1904, had specially provided that, when any section of the line was completed, the Government would be authorized to enter into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific for its operation. Its operation would be carried on pending the completion of the whole road. I think the House will agree with me that that would have been of very considerable importance to the province of New Brunswick, and I speak of that province because for something like two years t'he Transcontinental railway has been completed in New Brunswick from Moncton to Edmundston, or, indeed, a point somewhere northwest of Edmundston. of Parliament. When the vote was under consideration I called attention again to the statute of 1904. What was the offer that was made to you?

The offer that Mr. Hays made to us was to operate the section in New Brunswick just as soon as it was completed to Edmundston, or any other section, put on their rolling stock, keep an account of the operating expenses, that to be subject to examination by an accountant on behalf of the Government, and if there should be any deficit in the operation that deficit should be added to the capital account, and the company should pay interest upon it just as they do upon the cost of the Transcontinental railway.

That would be provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Well, nothing was said about that. Anything of that kind would come under the head of operating expenses. They agreed to see that any

If the Government had taken the matter up with the Girand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, I have not a shadow of doubt that during last year and this year that company would 'be operating the line in a satisfactory way. We have the evidence before us that the Government has degraded the Eastern Division of the Transcontinetal railway, that it has raised the grade and thereby lowered the standard of construction, and that it has done this without the consent of the Chief Engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific and in violation of the solemn agreement which was entered into between the company and the Government when the work of construction began. In view of the long and inexcusable delay which has taken place at the port of Quebec which is to be the St. Lawrence terminus of the Grand Trunk Pacific; in view of the inexcusable delay which has taken place at the port of St. John, I believe that the Government is worthy of censure and that this amendment ought to be passed.
There is another matter. I observe in the Supplementary Estimates that one million dollars is provided to make connection between the city of Montreal and the Transcontinental railway. I presume that is intended to allow the Government to engage in construction itself, instead of the construction which a company has been proposing to engage in. As to the port of St. John, I know as a matter of fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company were anxious either to have a branch from Chip-man down to St. John, which could be built at a comparatively small expense, or to utilize the railway to be built down the St. John Valley. The late Government had in contemplation, and so provided, that the St. John Valley line should be constructed from the city of St. John to Grand Falls, up to the standard of the Transcontinental railway, so that it might be used by the Grand Trunk Pacific as a means of bringing traffic to the port of St. John. are giving a subsidy to the Valley road and they are giving aid to the bridges, and they therefore are necessarily parties to the contract-the Government of New Brunswick has departed altogether from that idea, and the only portion of the line which is to be up to the standard of the Transcontinental is the portion between Fredericton and the city of St. John. For the whole distance extending north from Fredericton to Grand Falls, if they ever build as far as Grand Falls, the standard which was laid down in the first place has been absolutely departed from, and I am told that in many places there will be gradients as high as one and a half per cent. So that, as a means of getting to the port of St. John, this Valley road-upon which the Government of New Brunswick is lavishly guaranteeing the bonds, and to which this Government is giving large sums of money in the way of ordinary subsidies and the building of expensive bridges-will, notwithstanding this large expenditure, be an absolute failure as a factor to enable the trains of the Grand Trunk Pacific to get to the port of St. John; unless another branch is constructed which would connect the Valley line with the Transcontinental railway from Nabadogan to the city of Fredericton, which would require the expenditure of a very large additional sum of money.

It has been defeated in another way, because, although when the late Government was in office provision was made by this Parliament for a subsidy for a line all the way from St. John to Grand Falls, yet at the last session of Parliament, presumably at the request of the provincial Government, the subsidy for that portion of the line between Andover and Grand Falls was struck out, showing a clear intention on the part of this Government at all events and, if that action was taken at the instance of the provincial Government, showing the intention of the provincial Government also, that the portion of the line between Andover and Grand Falls should not be built. I appeal to members of the Government, I appeal to my horn, friend the Minister of

That is the provision in the original contract made by hon. gentlemen opposite, under which everything that has been carried on by the present Administration can be corrected and will be corrected at the proper time and in the proper place. I come back again to my hon. friend's reference to low rates between eastern and western Canada. How in Heaven's name can we have low rates upon the National Transcontinental railway when there are piled up against it such enormous fixed charges through the maladministration, extravagance and incompetency
10 p.m. of the late Administration in constructing the road. In the West we have an unlimited territory-hundreds of millions of acres of the finest land the world has ever known. Every year sees an increase in its production. Last year western Canada produced its greatest crop, and I am glad to know that this year there are millions of acres more under cultiva-

tion that in any previous year, leading us to hope for a largely increased production. That being the case, the people of western Canada are naturally most interested in the welfare of this great undertaking, and it is because of that interest that we are giving consideration to its construction and operation in every detail. It is because of conditions in the West that we deplore the fact that this line was so constructed as to make it impossible for the people of western Canada to ever hope to secure relief by way of reduced rates on the Transcontinental owing to its enormous fixed charges resulting from the maladministration to which I have referred. My hon. friend talks about the degrading of this line. Let me say that the degrading of this line began the day the specifications under which it was constructed were framed. The road was degraded the day it was started. The specification made it impossible for the road to be of that value to the people of Canada that it otherwise would have been. The specifications were so framed that three apparently simple words were largely the cause of the deplorable conditions in which' the people of Canada find themselves to-day in regard to this road. I will quote to the House the three words to which I refer: masses, best, judgment. Those three words have destroyed the value of the Transcontinental to the people of this country. Under the specifications we have this wording in regard to classification:
Solid rock excavation will include all rock found in ledges or masses of more than one cubic yard, which, in the judgment of the engineer, may be best removed by blasting.
After the first contracts were let, difficulty at once arose over the meaning of the word ' masses '. The contract price for solid rock was $1.50 to $1.70 per yard; loose rock fifty to sixty cents a yard; and common excavation about thirty cents a yard. The great difficulty was as to the meaning of the word * masses '. The chief engineer of that day found great difficulty in getting his district engineers to understand what the word * masses ' was meant to convey in these specifications. The examination of Mr. Lumsden shows that the greatest difficulty he had was to make his district engineers understand that the word ' masses ' meant rock. The district engineers did not agree with Mr. Lumsden, and were ready to classify as masses, frozen earth, gravel and almost anything that could be assembled in masses. A contro-

versy arose, and as a result a meeting was held at La Tuque in the province of Quebec at which the chief engineer and -several of his district engineers were present. The chief engineer gave as clearly and forcibly as he could his interpretation of this particular clause.
He found that the commissioners agreed with the district or local engineers, and they placed a very wide interpretation upon these specifications as laid down in the clause. The chief engineer apparently could not make any impression on the commissioners who sided with the local engineers, and when he returned to Ottawa he concluded to present his views to the Government of that day. Mr. Lnmsden did so. He presented first to the commissioners his interpretation of this clause, and he presented evidence of the fact that the treasury of this country was being plundered to an enormous extent as the result of the interpretation which was being made by the district engineers on the various portions of the line. He presented that view to the commissioners as strongly as he could, and the commissioners in turn transmitted the matter to the Government for their consideration. The Government of that day cannot claim that they did not have the facts placed before them, or that they had not knowledge of the conditions under which the public treasury was being plundered in the construction of this National Transcontinental railway in such a manner as to discount its usefulness to the people of Canada for all time to come as a means of reducing railway freight rates. What did the Government -do? They received that communication and returned it to the commissioners saying: We approve of the specifications; go on and carry out your work. I claim that the Government of that day were responsible, and that they were answerable to the people of the country for having committed the greatest crime that has ever been committed against the people of any country in respect to the building of this Transcontinental railway. We had notice of these conditions served upon the commissioners, and we had notice served on all and sundry of the people in various parts of this country that there was easy money to be made in the building of the Transcontinental railway. That being the condition, could we expect any other state of things than that which has been disclosed in the building of this line?

Is it any wonder that because of the maladministration of the late Government we have reason to regret the deplorable conditions under which the National Transcontinental railway has been built?
A good deal has been said about the development of our national ports, and let me say that if there is one part of the policy of the present Administration of which we have more reason to be proud than another, it is that we have shown energy, good will, and desire for the building up of our national ports, not only on the Atlantic but on the Pacific. The difference between hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in power and the Government of the day is, that in connection with all great national undertakings for the welfare of the country, whether it be the

port of St. John or the port of Halifax, or the port of Quebec, or the port of Montreal, or Toronto, or Hamilton, or Port William, or Vancouver, or Victoria, we can claim pride in the fact that we have the same policy in every port and every part of this Dominion. There is the difference between us and hon. gentlemen opposite, who have one policy for St. John, another for Halifax, another for Montreal, and another for every section of the country where they, in their limited and mistaken judgment think they may gain a few votes in the hope of getting back to power. But our position is different; whether it be in respect to the development of our prairies, or whether it be in respect to the development of every port and every part of Canada, we stand for a broad national policy which conserves to our people their own trade within the borders of their own country. We stand by a policy which conserves to all Canadians, whether this be their native land or their adopted country, the results of the fruits of their own industry, and the development of our natural resources in the best interests of all our people. That is the policy which this Government has stood by in the past, and that is the policy which this Government will stand by in the future. We shall develop in the future as in the past our great national ports. We shall push forward the early completion of the National Transcontinental railway in the hope that the unfavourable conditions which we have inherited from our predecessors may be made to disappear under wise, and prudent, and honest administration, so that this railway will confer on the country the benefits it ought to. In view of all this, I ask hon. members to vote down the motion of my hon. friend from St. John, as being of no force and no effect, and of no value to the people of Canada. In order to get to them, he has had to get the right of way for some two miles from the Canadian Northern and for two miles from the Canadian Pacific. I believe that at the present time he is trying to enter into an agreement. There is no use in denying the facts, because they are as I have stated.	I believe that the	Government have running rights over the Canadian Pacific; I believe that part of the contract has been made; but so far as I know no contract has been made with the Canadian Northern, and we are still in the air as to that. This matter is not new. We had the same condition of affairs last year, and on the 29th of May this is how I spoke in regard to the matter:
At present the Grand Trunk Pacific is brought from Sillery to the Champlain market. Then there is to be a track built from the Champlain market to the tracks now owned by the Canadian Pacific railway. All this presupposes that there has been first, some agreement between the commission and the harbour commissioners, to build that track of railway, and also an agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway to use their tracks. Then, on the other side, on St. Charles river, I understood my hon. friend to say that the Grand Trunk Pacific were to use the tracks of the Canadian Northern railway. Is that so?
Mr. Cochrane: Tes.
Therefore it is very clear that this is not the Transcontinental.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: Then, that presupposes another agreement with the Canadian Northern railway. Have all these agreements been consummated, or are they merely contemplated?
Mr. Cochrane: The heads of the agreements have been arrived at.

Sir Wilfrid Laurier: That is not very satisfactory.
Mr. Cochrane: The principles are agreed upon, and there will not be much detail to work out.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: That is not our experience. However, if the city council of Quebec are satisfied, I have nothing more to say.
Mr. Pelletier: They are unanimous.
Wc had there the statement of the Min-isiter of Railways that the department were negotiating for the acquisition of that line of railway. On the 6th of this month of June I was told by the acting Minister of Railways, that although this matter was in contemplation, the agreement had not been consummated. I was told that the matter had been agreed upon, but that no writing had been done, and I understand that no writing has been done up to date. Therefore we are in the same position to-day as we were a year ago. My hon. friend the Postmaster General stated last year, and he repeated it again this year, that the people in Quebec were quite satisfied with the condition of things. The people of Quebec will be satisfied with anything, provided it is done. What they want is to have terminals, workshops, a station and everything else so that the road will be operated; but up to the present time the people of Quebec have been subjected to disappointment after disappointment; they have been fed on promises, not one of which has yet been fulfilled.
Perhaps the right hon. gentleman will explain what he did between 1903 and 1911 in Quebec.

Here is the
eternal statement:	What have you done
during eight years? We were told a moment ago by the Minister of Public Works that we were ignominiously defeated because we did nothing. What are you doing? Nothing. We made a contract and built the railway. What we had done by 1911 was this:	We had the plans for the
shops at Cap Rouge.
That took eight years.

Yes; and it
was undone Iby the present Government, who in three years have not been able to sign an agreement, although they have changed the location of the shops. This is what has made the people of Quebec more disappointed than they have ever been before, namely, that they have been fed on promises, and that nothing has been done.
An agreement was entered into by the late Government with the city of Quebec

for the acquiring of a site for a new station. The city of Quebec agreed to sell to the late Government at the nominal price of $100,000 property which was of great value, in order to have the station at that place. My hon. friend the Postmaster General tells us that the station was wrongly located. All I have to say to my hon. friend is that the location was determined only after consultation with all the railway companies whose lines communicate with the city of Quebec-with the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk, the Quebec Central, the Intercolonial, the Quebec and St. John, the Delaware and Hudson.; which railways all approved the location of the new station. In the face of these conditions, this agreement was cancelled and another made with the Canadian Pacific railway for the construction of a union station. The correspondence on this point does not show that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company ever agreed to that change; on the contrary, it shows that they protested against it all along. When first communicated with on the subject, Mr. Chamberlin -said: if a proper plan is submitted to us, we do not say that we will not accept it- But when the plan was submitted to them they had the greatest objection to it. In view of what has taken place, it may be worth while reading to the House a few of the objections set forth in a letter written by Mr. Chamberlin to Major Leonard on August 9, 1913:
Dear Major Leonard,-Referring to your communication relative to proposed contract with the Canadian Pacific railway for use of joint terminals in Quebec, would say that this contract has been carefully examined by myself and other officers of the company and we do not regard the proposed agreement as at all satisfactory from the standpoint of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Generally speaking, the whole scheme of the agreement is objectionable inasmuch as It places the entire control of the terminals in the hands of the Canadian Pacific railway-to illustrate:
Clause 2. Under this the Transcontinental is permitted by the Canadian Pacific to use the joint tracks and joint premises in conjunction with the Pacific Company and any other company to which the Pacific Company may grant similar privileges. As pointed out by Vice-President Kelley, under this the Canadian Pacific railway might entirely exclude the Grand Trunk or in fact any other company except that operating or having running rights over the Transcontinental railway.
Clause 4. This provides that the Transcontinental shall acquire certain lands and lease them in perpetuity to the Canadian Pacific. This certainly is rather a strange provision requiring as it does that the Government shall
acquire land for terminal purposes and then transfer not only the property but the entire control over to the Canadian Pacific railway.
In view of this extraordinary statement on the part of Mr. Chamberlin, it may be well if we look for a moment at clause 4 of the contract. It is as follows:
The Transcontinental shall, as soon as conveniently may be, acquire the lands edged in yellow on the said plan, and shall lease such lands to the Pacific Company during the term of this agreement, at an annual rental equal to four and one-half per centum per annum of the cost of the said lands, which cost shall include all expenses of and incidental to the acquisition thereof, and the Pacific Company shall hold the same for the use and benefit of the parties hereto, under the provisions of this agreement.
This is the extraordinary part of this agreement. The Government is to buy lands for the purpose of the joint station and this land is to be transferred in perpetuity to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, so that the Government railway becomes an adjunct of the Canadian Pacific railway; a second fiddle, as it were, and not by any means master of the situation. Mr. Chamberlin goes on:
Clause 5. This only provides for the setting apart for joint use of such additional lands as in the opinion of the parties may be required. The Canadian Pacific railway being one of the parties could under this simply decline to concur in any suggestion made by the Transcontinental Commission with the result that the clause would become ineffectual.
Clause 6. The same remarks apply to this clause, which is further objectionable inasmuch as it provides that the Canadian Pacific may rearrange, rebuild, alter or make improvements, additions or extensions to the joint premises without the leave or consent of the other parties interested.
Clause 7. By this all switching and shunting service is to be performed by the Pacific Company.
Mr. Chamberlin concludes as follows:
I do not know how the Transcontinental Commission regard these clauses, but to my mind the Grand Trunk Pacific, as lessee of the eastern division, could not under any circumstances accept them and expect to be placed in anything like as favourable a position in the use of these joint terminals as the Canadian Pacific railway would be. In my opinion, the terminals should, as at Winnipeg, be placed under the control of a terminals board, or, what would perhaps be better, should be conveyed to a terminal company to be incorporated with powers somewhat similar to above conferred upon the Toronto Terminals Railway Company, and the Ottawa Terminals Railway Company. As you are no doubt aware, the Canadian Pacific railway have never been satisfied with the terms of the Toronto Union station agreement of 1892 because they considered that under it the Grand Trunk had too much control. It is for that reason, as I understand it, that they now practically insist that the union terminals at Toronto shall

be owned and controlled by a terminals company. The same reasoning should apply to Quebec as well as to Toronto.
These were the reasons why the Grand Trunk Pacific company refused to agree to the contract which was made between the commission and the Canadian Pacific railway in regard to the union station. I put it to the judgment of any man in this House; can any fault be found with the reasons given by Mr. Chamberlin for refusing to become a party to that contract ? Mr. Chamberlin says: I cannot agree to that contract because the Government is going to cause the National Transcontinental to become tributory to the Canadian Pacific railway. Attention was called by the hon. member for the city of St. John to the enormous difficulty which may arise from the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific is not bound to lease this railway. You have given them the power to refuse to take the railway, and no man in this House will pretend that they will agree to a contract made with the Canadian Pacific railway behind their backs. No man will pretend that the Grand Trunk Pacific can be forced to take over the railway; it is evident that if they choose to do so, they may refuse to operate it. What will be the consequence ? The consequence will be that grave difficulties will arise, and heaven only knows how they will end. All this was done under what was termed to be a business Government. One would have expected that this Government would have taken precautions to make no mistakes; but it has degraded the road, and, in violation of the contract which was made in 1903, which provided that everything should be done jointly with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, has changed the sites of the workshops and stations without consulting the Grand Trunk Pacific company.
But that is not all. Hon. gentlemen opposite promised the people of Quebec that all these works would be completed within a very short time. At a sitting of the City Council of Quebec on May 22, a resolution was passed protesting against the character of the work and the delay in executing it, as follows:
That on the 26th of August, 1910, the city of Quebec sold to the Transcontinental Commission the Champlain market, which is in the central part of the lower town of the city of Quebec, a property of very great value for the nominal sum of $100,000 under the express condition, which was the main consideration of the contract, that the Transcontinental should build, without delay, a passenger station of great value with suitable buildings and approaches of a value of at least two millions, not including the
[Sir Wilfrid Laurier.i
cost of the expropriations of the lands required ;
That the said Transcontinental Commission has since demolished the building of the Champlain market, thus depriving the city of its most important market place and compelling the city to procure, at great expense.
I shall not read all of it. The conclusion is:
That the council of the city of Quebec emphatically disapproves the mode of action of the Chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, which is contrary to the interest of the city, and that His Worship the Mayor is hereby instructed to notify the Prime Minister of Canada, the Minister of Railways and the Hon. L. P. Pelletier, representing the district of Quebec, of the manner in which the city of Quebec has been treated by the Transcontinental Commission with regard to the question of the terminus station, in contradiction with the policy of the Government as publicly and solemnly declared by the Right Hon. R. L. Borden, Prime Minister, last fall, at the public dinner tendered to him by the citizens of Quebec and confirmed in the correspondence exchanged between the members of the Government and His Worship the Mayor on this subject, and especially by a letter of the Prime Minister to the Mayor, bearing date the 24th of January, 1914.
His Worship the Mayor in his explanation having referred to a letter of the Right Hon. R. L. Borden, Prime Minister, addressed to him on the 24th January last, 1914, and containing important declarations and statements, it is ordered : that a summary of the said declarations and statements be inscribed in the minutes of this meeting as follows, to wit:
1. The union station: agreement for construction and operation settled and agreements signed. Contract expected to he let by the Canadian Pacific railway at a very early date.
This statement is clear. The agreement between the Government and the Canadian Pacific railway has been concluded; it has been signed; it is ready for execution; it was to be executed; the contract was to be let at a very early date. This was on the 24th of January. We are now at the 8th of June, and so far nothing has been done towards the lettmg of the contract. I do not know that even the plane have been prepared. I am not informed that tenders have been let. I am not aware that the city council has been informed that the plans have been approved. 1 inquired lately from them whether the plans of the Canadian Pacific railway had been submitted, and I was told that they had not been. I understand, also, that the Board of Trade recently applied to the Canadian Pacific railway to ascertain when they would commence the building of that station, and the only answer was that it would be done in due time. That was all the comfort they got. So far

nothing has been done. No wonder that there is a great deal of discontent in the city of Quebec to-day. My hon. friend the Postmaster General made the statement a few days ago that the people of Quebec were satisfied with the changes, but that there was discontent because the commissioner, Major Leonard, had been slow in carrying on the work. The people of Quebec have been in this matter extremely generous and extremely forbearing. I do not admit that they have been satisfied with the changes made. They have accepted the changes suggested by the Government. They agreed to have the union station; but they di<l_ so under a reasonable expectation that this work would be commenced and completed at an early date. But I venture to say with great confidence that, if the people had anticipated that there would have been such delay as there has been, three years having elapsed before the work was completed, they would never have given consent to the changed site of the station. This journal goes on summarizing the letter of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister:
Champlain market station: Minister of Railways informs that plans will be completed next week and action taken immediately after without the slightest unnecessary delay.
That was on the 24th of January. The plans were not all completed until the middle of May, and the notices for tenders were sent out within the last fifteen days, or thereabouts.
Sir, what is the kind of station that we shall have at the Champlain market? The contract by which the city of Quebec sold the market to the Government said in so many words that one of the reasons why they sold that property, which is of great value, as everybody knows, for $100,000, which was simply a nominal sum, was that a station of great value was to be placed there. And a few days ago we had before us the plan of the station to be placed on the Champlain market, and it is what? It is a building which will cost but $70,000, a brick building of the most modest proportions, something which is simply unworthy of the city of Quebec; and I must protest, on behalf of the city of Quebec, that it is treating that city with contempt to place such a building as that beneath the walls of the city, where it will be daily in evidence to all comers. We should have something in keeping with the grandeur of the enterprise. But
the people of Quebec will have to take what is offered them. This process verbal goes on to say:
Tunnel: construction will be undertaken as mentioned in banquet. Connection with Canadian Northern at Cap Rouge entering St. Charles side of the city will he ready for traffic when road ready for operation.
I do not know what was mentioned at the banquet, but I understand my hon. friend stated that the tunnel would be constructed at a very early date, as it was part of the work that was necessary for the terminals of the Grand Trunk Pacific at Quebec. I think that nothing has been done up to the present time towards the construction of the tunnel. I understand that correspondence has been exchanged between Major Leonard, of the National Transcontinental railway, and Mr. Chamberlin, the president of the Grand Trunk, the effect of which is that it is proposed to delay the construction of the tunnel. It has been stated, and I have not seen it denied-if it is not so I shall be glad to hear from the Prime Minister or the Postmaster General-that it is not intended to construct the tunnel at an early date, as stated at the Quebec banquet. My hon,. friend the Postmaster General knows as well as I do, because he represents the county of Quebec, that without the tunnel the union station is absolutely of no use to the Transcontinental. A train coming from the West must come to the riveT front at Champlain market, and there must be a tunnel for that purpose. That is the condition of things which exists today in the city of Quebec and no wonder the people are disappointed, no wonder they are sore and sick of heart. What excuse has the Government to offer for such delay as has occurred? What can be said to the people of Quebec for delaying this work from day to day and from year to year? Before we leift office in 1911 we had given a contract for the building of a station at Champlain market at a cost of $1,000,000. I heard the Postmaster General say the other day that the station would not be of any use as it would occupy so much ground that there would be none left between the station and the cliff for the building of lines. I may say that that consideration has been given attention by other men more competent than my hon. friend. It was taken into consideration by all the railway companies to which I alluded a moment ago. Al'l the railway companies that come to Quebec had agreed to that station, and my hon. friend says that it

would be of no use. Why the plans were changed passes my comprehension. I know the value of a union station. It has been admitted by many cities that it is better to have one union station than two or three independent ones. My hon. friend the Postmaster General knows that the topographical conditions of Quebec make it impossible to have a union station except at great cost. You may have a union station, it is true, but it will add greatly to the cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific and be inconveniently situated. A union station on the cliff near the Plains of Abraham would have been much more conveniently situated for passenger traffic, but that is not being done. The station is being placed in the valley of the St. Charles river: The Grand Trunk Pacific is. in the valley of St. Lawrence, and between those rivers there is a cliff at least 200 feet high which has to be overcome, and which makes a tunnel absolutely necessary. The Prime Minister gave his pledge to the people of Quebec that within a very short time this station would be built, but six months have passed and he has yet taken no stepsto redeem his promise. That is the way Quebec has been treated right along, and no wonder the people are sore. But it is not a matter 11 p.m. of disappointment simply to the people of Quebec; they are not the only people interested. The whole of Canada is vitally interested in this project, and unless a station is built at Quebec the Grand Trunk Pacific will be of no value whatever. The Minister of Public Works said a moment ago that it was a mistake ever to have built this Transcontinental, but I say if ever a work was needed it was the building of this road, and I believe that that question whenever submitted to the Canadian people will be approved as it always has been approved whenever submitted to them. But the railway can be of no value unless all the necessary works are completed.
To sum up what I have said, it was a mistake to change the station from Champlain Market to the St. Charles river. It was a mistake to change the shops from near the bridge to St. Malo. That is my judgment in view of the interests of the road, but I submit to what has been done. One thing, however, we have a right to hope for, and not only to hope for but to exact from this Government, and that is that having made these changes they must carry them out without any delay whatever.

The right hon. gentleman has made a very eloquent plea indeed. He has practically confined his remarks to the Quebec situation, but has touched en passant on the question of the so-called degradation of the road. He has told us that the Minister of Public Works admitted the degradation. I do not think the people of this country can be led astray on this question. It is a question whether this road could not have been better constructed some other way from the one adopted. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) made a great speech on that question-probably the best of his life. He gave us quotations and opinions supporting his views; but there are opinions to the contrary, and whether the principle of momentum grades is right or wrong, I think the hon. member for South Renfrew will admit that it pays to have momentum grades during the time of construction, and that if necessary they can be levelled down after the road is completed more cheaply than during construction.
I do not admit that at all; I contend to the contrary absolutely.
Does my hon. friend deny that momentum grades are very often used, and that it is good railway practice to remove these grades after the line has been completed?

I have consulted a good many authorities on that point. Where a road has very heavy gradients like the Canadian Pacific railway had, and it is impossible to overcome them, it is good railway practice even in this country to introduce momentum grades as they reduce the ruling grades where they are heavy. But the best engineers I have consulted- and if I did not give this information to the House before, it was in my hands- maintain that it costs much more to remedy these degradations after the road has been completed than it would cost to remedy them during construction. It is obvious that after the road has been opened for traffic the trains would be seriously interfered with by ballast trains wiping out these momentum grades. These construction trains could only work at certain intervals, and consequently the cost of remedying the degradations would be much higher than if done during construction.

I would like to say for the information of my hon. friend that only

this morning the chief engineer of the Transcontinental told me that this work could be carried out after completion of the road for one-third less what it would cost during construction.

That is not the opinion of the engineers whom I have consulted. I think it is only reasonable to expect that the work could be done more cheaply during construction than after completion of the road, when the work could only be done at intervals.

Engineers may differ, but at all events the opinion of the engi-. n.eer appointed by my hon. friend should have some weight. Mr. Gordon Grant was not appointed by us; he was chief engineer of the Transcontinental when we came into power, and as the Minister of Public Works has just said, it is his opinion that this work can be done much more cheaply after the completion of the road.
My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) says himself that it is a question of opinion amongst engineers. Let us take it that way. Engineers will differ on that question as lawyers will differ on certain questions, but >at all events there is one point about which nobody has differed and that is that these grades, if they are not proper ones, can be remedied at any time. That cannot be controverted, that cannot ibe gainsaid. Now we have the opinion of the man under whose direction, as chief engineer, these things were done, and who tells us that they can be remedied for a bagatelle of $200,000.

Then they must be
remedied?

Nobody has ever
pretended that there are not certain grades which are not according to the specifications, but as my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) has said, there was a great hurry to finish the road *and it will be admitted by every one that it would take less time to construct a road with these temporary grades than it would have taken to build a road at once with grades of .04 per cent. Where is the great crime about that? There is none. These things are going to be remedied; they are going to be put in final shape. Whatever bon. gentlemen may say against this Government in that respect, at all events it cannot he alleged as a reason why the Grand Trunk Pacific will not take the road over.
Let us come to the remarks made by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) about the Quebec terminals. The Quebec terminals have been the subject of discussion for some time, and the remarks made to-night by my right hon. friend are only a reproduction in more eloquent form of many articles published by the Liberal newspapers in Quebec. What is the situation in that respect? I have made several statements in the House on this matter and I am going to take it up briefly to-night so that there will be no misunderstanding about it. The plans which had been prepared for the Quebec terminal and station were: in the minds of almost every good citizen of Quebec, impossible of realization from the point of view of busibess and the public interest. Everybody knew that these plans had been adopted for a certain, purpose which nobody could guess, but many of the best political friends of my right hon. friend were themselves absolutely of the opinion that this station could not be built as it had been planned. This station, as mapped out under the former Government, was to be the sole and only terminal for this big Transcontinental railway. I will appeal to any one of common sense who knows the city of Quebec, and knows the space between the cliff and the river front, to say whether, both from the engineering and business point of view, this was the proper place for the terminal of the National Transcontinental railway. Surely, for a terminal and station of that kind you must have space. You must have space for freight sheds, for yards and for a great number of cars near the station. Any one who had seen the proposed site, any school child, would come to the conclusion that it was absolutely impossible to erect a big railway station .at that point. When this question was discussed before the late Government resigned, many Liberals promised the people of Quebec that the situation would be remedied in some way. The city council adopted the proposition because they were told that they must do it, but let my right hon. friend ask the mayor of Quebec, who is one of his best political friends, whether our proposition is a better one than his and I will stand by the answer. That is a fair proposition to make. My right hon. friend will never put that question to the mayor of Quebec because he knows, and because the mayor of Quebec has told him-
No.

Well, if he has not he is prepared to tell him at any time my right hon. friend wants to know. Instead of that impracticable proposition it is proposed to have the big union station in the division represented in the House of Commons by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. He is dead against it, he says he wants it on the Champlain market which is not at all in the heart and centre of the city, which is far away from the centre and business quarter of the city, which is far away from one of the leading commercial business thoroughfares, St. Joseph street, right in the heart of my hon. friend's constituency. I say that the place for the union station is in the heart of the city as the city is built now. I have to fight in this House in order to have this station in the heart and the centre ot the city and I have to fight that battle against the gentleman who represents that constituency in the House of Commons. That is the stand which he has taken and in which he persists. I was going to ask him whether he was prepared to stand here in the House of Commons and tell us that he preferred the Champlain Market station to the Palais station in his own constituency tout he has relieved me of the necessity of putting that question to him because he has made that declaration two or three times to-night in the course of his speech. He does not want to have that station where the business men and his own friends and supporters unanimously want to have it placed, he is against them, he is fighting against the realization of their will and desire though he is their representative in this Parliament. That is the situation and anybody who knows anything about the condition of public opinion in the city of Quebec will corroborate the statement that I am making.
Now, let us come to the shops. There again we have committed a great crime. What is that crime? We are told that the late Government had done a great thing, that during the eight years which elapsed between 1903 and 1911 they had accomplished the marvellous feat of buying a plot of land. We are told to-night by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition that these shops should have been located at this place which is eight or nine miles from Quebec. We have changed the plans and we have located the shops in or near the

city of Quebec, and we have located them in the constituency represented by the right hon. gentleman himself, and where nintey-nine out of every one hundred of his electors want to see those shops erected. As a matter of fact, the right hon. gentleman is about the only man who opposes that change. I defy him to go to Quebec and get from his own electors a petition signed-and if he gets one-third of his electors to ask that these shops should be continued to be located at Cap Rouge, I shall stand by that decision and I shall ask that they be changed back to Cap Rouge. Let my right hon. friend try that.
In speaking as I do to-night I know as well as any one can know that in locating those shops at St. Malo we have met the views and desires of almost every good citizen in Quebec, and particularly of the electors of Quebec East, who are represented by this very gentleman who fights against the unanimous desire of his own electors. We are told by the right hon. gentleman that these shops should have been built at Cap Rouge, nine miles from Quebec, so that they would be on the line of tire Transcontinental railway. He tells us that these shops should not be in Quebec or near Quebec, because they will not be on the line of the railway. Does the right hon. gentleman mean that the National Transcontinental railway is not going to enter Quebec at all, because he says that to have the shops established on the line of the road we must have them nine miles outside of Quebec. Surely his desire is that the Transcontinental railway should enter Quebec, and if it does enter Quebec, then by putting the shops in or near Quebec, we can get them by one means or another located on the line of the National Transcontinental. If that be so, there is nothing left of his argument except that he might want the railway to pass over the Quebec bridge, nine miles from Quebec and go to Portland or some other place.
Hear, hear.

It is time for hon.
gentlemen opposite to say, hear, hear; but they should think this matter over. We shall hear more of this matter later and we shall have the opinion of the people of Quebec on it at some time or another, and then we shall know who was right and who was wrong. I assume the full responsibility before the House, and before the coun-

try, and before the electors of my right hon. friend, for this change, and I am prepared to stand by their decision on the question. This will be one of the issues which will be raised when the people have an occasion to pronounce upon it.
You will be defeated just the same.
Will the elections be soon?
They may be sooner than the hon. member would like.
I have no fear.
As to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau), I would not exchange the chances I have to come back here with his. Let him wait and see.
I am waiting for you.
Is that an invitation?
Any time you like I am ready.	.
Then it will be fully considered.
You are not accepting.
Just wait and see.

Vou will not be
elected.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. the Postmaster General has the floor, and he is entitled to a hearing without interruption.
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

We were told by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition that all the railways had agreed to the location of that station at Champlain market, and although the newspapers stated it many times, the people of Quebec had doubts about it. One of the first things I did after the elections of 1911 was to ask the Canadian Pacific railway whether that statement were true, and the answer given me by the Canadian Pacific railway was that it was preposterous to think of a union station at the Champlain market, and that they had not even considered the question. The gentleman who gave me that answer was Mr. McNichol, and it was confirmed to me by Sir Thomas Shaugnessey.
My right hon. friend said that all the railways had accepted the Champlain Mar-321
ket station, but if it was a station only for the Grand Trunk Pacific, what. business had the other railways to accept it or refuse it ? Why were the other railways brought into consultation if they had no business in the matter. We were told in Quebec that this was going to be a union station, and with a blare of trumpets the Hon. Mr. Parent called together the heads of the railway companies, and we were told they had met and considered the situation and that they had all agreed that Champlain market was the proper place to build a station. To-night for the first time I have heard from the right hon. gentleman that it was not intended that Champlain market should Ibe a union station, but if that be so why were the other railway companies asked to confer about it? I shall wait for the answer before I proceed further.
Now, as a matter of fact, all the railway men who have been consulted by me told me that Mr. Parent had asked them about it, but as they were not concerned they would not take any part in the discussion. They said that the Champlain market was no place for a station, and that they would not go there, but that as Mr. Parent wanted to have it there they had nothing to say about it. And yet that is the great argument which the right hon. gentleman has put forward this session, and last session, and the session before, in order to-justify the choice of the Champlain market.
We are told this Government has not kept faith with the people of Quebec so far as this station is concerned. The hon. member for Quebec Centre (Mr. Lachance) said something like that the other day, and it was really very amusing to hear him say so, in view of the fact that we have entered into a contract between the Government, the Transcontinental Railway Commission and the city of Quebec, which is in black and white. There is not one item or one line in that contract about the station at Champlain market.
