This contract asks for the building of a union station at the Palais, and the building of the shops at St. Malo has been assented to at the request of the mayor of Quebec and of the members of the city council of Quebec, the majority of whom are Liberals.
They are the people who have asked for that. The mayor of Quebec came here with several aldermen, and, in my presence, they put to the Minister of Railways and the Chairman of the Transcontinental Commission their request that the shops should be located at St. Malcr, near Quebec. This was



done at their request. Why make so many exaggerations about the matter now? When the Government succeeded in having the shops located at St. Malo, a contract was entered into under which the covenants of the former contract entered into by Mr. Parent were put to one side, and under which the Government undertook to build a union station with the Canadian Pacific and to locate the shops at St. Malo. Under that contract the city of Quebec consented to give the use of certain streets, and to grant exemption of taxes for twenty years, and certain privileges in regard to water taxes as well. My right hon. friend, a member for the city of Quebec, just like the hon. member for Quebec centre (Mr. Lachance), have taken so little interest in this matter; they have put so little of their heart into it that they do not know even what the covenants of the contracts are, and they speak of the Cnamplain market as 'being one o.f the contractual obligations. I will tell my right hon. friend that it is not one. The contract with the city of Quebec will be fulfilled when the union station is built, and the Champlain Market station is being built by the Government over and above the bargain which we have made with the city of Quebec. I want the right hon. gentleman to know that to-night for the first time, because he has evidently never heard of it before.' He has taken his information from old papers and from his own Liberal paper in Quebec, whose mission, as well as whose very life, is to lie every day of the year in regard to the matter; and I am not surprised, if his information has been taken from the columns of that paper, that my right hon. friend and the member for Quebec have so little information in regard to the matter. The Champlain Market station is something which the Government have given to Quebec, and which they are not obliged to give to Quebec. I cannot repeat that too often in order to make the people understand the matter, which is apparently so little understood by the gentlemen who represent here the city of Quebec.
My right 'hon. friend has read a resolution from the city council of Quebec in which complaints are made that this work has not been begun sooner. This resolu tion was passed, I think, about the middle of May; it does not contain one iota of complaint against the Government; and without boasting, I think I can venture to say that the people of Quebec understand that they owe something to this Govern-

ment by whom they have been taken care of as they never were before during the fifteen years of the Liberal regime.
What have you done?

A resolution was
passed complaining of the Chairman of the Transcontinental. When the spring came, *the people of Quebec expected that the works which were not under way would be started. They were not started, and the people complained and rightly so. I am not going to make any subterfuge about the matter. I think these works should have begun earlier this spring. The people are unanimously of that opinion, and I agree with them. We succeeded in starting the shops last fall; and we succeeded in starting many other great public works in Quebec, which were -sorely and badly neglected by my right hon. friend. The Champlain Market station should have been started as soon as the snow left the ground; and although that was not done, it was started as soon as possible, and I have the pleasure to read for the information of the House and of the people of Quebec the following letter:
Dear Mr. Pelletier:
For your information, I may say that I have to-day written to the commission recommending that the tender for the erection of the Champlain Market station be awarded to Mr. Joseph Gosselin, of L6vis, Quebec, who is the lowest tenderer for the work. I am just in receipt of a telegram from Mr. Leonard authorizing my recommendation to the letting of this contract be forwarded to the Government. It will he sent over to-morrow. I have wired Doucet-
That is the district engineer.
__to lay out the work and instruct Gosselin to
go ahead.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) Gordon Grant,
Chief Engineer.
That is another thing that this Government have started when, during the long fifteen years of the Liberal regime, there was never anything started. We have started things now, and they are going to be carried to completion.
What is the amount of that contract?

I am not in a position to tell my hon. friend.
My right hon. friend has complained that the Grand Trunk Pacific are not giving their consent to the plans and to the changes. I have answered that so often that I have reason to be surprised that it is brought up again. To prove his theory my right

hon. friend has read a letter signed by Mr. Chamberlin, dated the 9th of August, 1913. Why he should do that, I fail to understand. Mr. Chamberlin wrote that letter in the month of August, 1913; but the objections which he formulated in that letter were later on dealt with. He sent Mr. Biggar and Mr. Kelley to Ottawa.
Mr. Beattie of the Canadian Pacific railway was there, and Mr. Dalrymple of the Grand Trunk railway.
All these objections were taken up one by one, and were settled to the satisfaction of the Grand Trunk railway people.
I moved for the correspondence, and it has not been brought down.	'
My right hon. friend was not there; I was.
I have asked for the correspondence.

Mr. Chamberlin has said many times to Mr. Cochrane and myself that he would like to have these plans submitted to him; but he has said: I will trust you. He has said in my presence to Mr. Cochrane on many occasions: I will trust you to decide those questions, and 1 am sure you will decide them in the best interest of the the country. He has said: What you will do, I shall be satisfied with. When this contract was entered into, Mr. Chamberlin complained of one thing. I asked him the other day again, and he said that he had agreed to what we had done; that that was all right; but he complained that he had not been notified that the papers had been signed. Of course, he may be right in this respect, and I will not enter into the difficulties which may have arisen between Mr. Chamberlin and Mr. Leonard; but that was his complaint. He said, however, as to the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company: My suggestions have been met; what have I to complain of ?
As regards the tunnel, we had that matter up again on Saturday. We have had it up on many occasions. My hon. friend said on Saturday that this tunnel would never be built.
A week-end matter.

Yes, that is a week-end matter. The Minister of Railways has said that this tunnel will be built. The acting
32 lj
Minister of Railways repeated that statement on Saturday on the floor of this House.
When will it be built ?

We are dealing now
with the Champlain market station, which is the most pressing subject at the moment, because we wish to have it ready when the road is completed. The construction of the shops will take some time, but they are under way and good progress is being made. The Prime Minister made a statement to this effect at Quebec in the month of October last; his word is as good as his bond, and the people of Quebec know it. It may be that the Grand Trunk Pacific will not take over the road when it is completed; I shall not at the moment discuss whether that would be a great blessing or a great calamity, but I do know that if the Grand Trunk Pacific Company has any objection to leasing the eastern section of the Transcontinental, the only cause of this objection will be that they will have to carry about their neck the millstone of the heavy cost of the Transcontinental. That is not guesswork; that I know is a fact. Anybody who confers with the Grand Trunk Pacific people will know that what I say is true. Not only is it true that they will find it a big proposition, in view of the cost of the road, to give reasonable freight rates, but the Grand Trunk railway, which is really the Grand Trunk Pacific, will have to consider whether or not they would ruin and wreck the Grand Trunk railway if they entered upon this lease. This is one of the points to which I particularly call my right hon. friend's attention. I say that the motion made by the hon. member for the city of St. John is not justified by the facts which I have related, which are well known and recognized as true by every one who has looked into this question. If there is any difficulty about this matter, the difficulty will be rightly laid at the door of the gentlemen who are responsible for the excessive cost of this railway. This railway will cost in the vicinity of $100,000 a mile. What railway company will, without a great deal of consideration and hesitation, undertake to operate a road under those conditions, paying interest on this very large outlay? That is a serious question and if the difficulty ever does arise the responsibility will rest with those who have built the road and who loudly complain about what we have done in respect of the Canadian Northern railway, which

cost $35,000 to $40,000 a mile, while the National Transcontinental cost $100,000 a mile.

There is some difference
not in only in the cost of these two roads, but in the quality as well.
Mr, PELLETIER: I do not know about that; when the Canadian Northern is completed, I think it will be one of the best roads not only in Canada but in America.
My hon. friend, perhaps inadvertently, did not answer the question put to him a moment ago: when will the work of the tunnel begin?

The work on the tunnel will begin as soon as possible. It will be begun quite in time for my hon. friend to be very much disappointed over the fact that it has been begun and that his party has lost more of its popularity in the city of Quebec.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the House will allow me to say a few words more this evening, though I have already spoken several times on the question of the Transcontinental, and particularly in regard to the condition in which the the property of that railway line is in the city of Quebec, since this Government reached power in the month of September, 1911.
In view of the statements and misstatements of facts made by the hon. Postmaster General in the speech he has just delivered, statements which are foundationless in many instances, I deem it my duty to address the House once more in order to set matters right.
There is one matter concerning which I shall at once let the minister know what are my views, as well as the views of the citizens of Quebec, Conservatives as well as Liberals; I refer to the attacks directed against the right hon. leader of the Opposition by the Postmaster General. The citizens of Quebec are in the same mood to-day as they were of yore, their hopes are the same, their faith and trust in our leader are unchanged.
The hon. Postmaster General thought it proper to voice a kind of protest and to state that in Quebec there might be surprises ip store for him. If there be surprises in store for any one, it is for the hon. Postmaster General who has taken the responsibility for all that happened, or rather fell short of happening, within the last three years. The Postmaster General is too 
shrewd to flatter himself with the hope of having prepared surprises for the leader of the Opposition in Quebec. However, should he deceive himself to that extent, I am bound to rid him of that false notion, and to assure him that his opinion will not count for much in our city as against the statements and opinions of the hon. leader of the Opposition. Though he may simulate indignation, I am in a position to state that the public feeling in Quebec is against him, especially in regard to the matter now under the consideration of the House, and it will assert itself in the proper place and time. There are numerous reasons for that. The hon. gentleman is a man of resources. When he has a case which is as good as lost, he endeavours to make believe that his opponent is open to almost any charge, and accordingly he takes on the airs of a man in a rage. Those who are well acquainted with him do not worry very much over it; they know that the only occasion for that exhibition of temper is the weakness of his case.
The Postmaster General told us he could not guess the reason why such terminal plans had been adopted by the Liberal Government previous to 1911. He must be the only one that is left in the dark; for every engineer has stated the reason. On the other hand, no one knows what can have induced this Government to agree to the changes effected in the plans since 1911.
True, the hon. Postmaster General insinuated that there were possibly improper motives that would explain the plans laid down for the [DOT] building of the original terminals. Insinuations are easily made, and I might reply that some people have insinuated in this connection that speculation was rife in connection with the changes effected in the last instance. I do not put very much faith in that kind of gossip and I prefer dealing with the question on its actual merit, which will not prevent the people of Quebec from wondering what justification there is for such changes. The hon. gentleman held the floor three-quarters of an hour without broaching the subject; last week, on several occasions, and also in the course of the debate on the report of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton he dealt with the subject, but without offering any satisfactory explanation. So far, accordingly, I see no reason why the leader of the Opposition should have lost the confidence of his constituents, as was claimed by the hon. Postmaster General. The latter gentleman has enough

to clear his skirts of without concerning himself with the welfare of the electors of Quebec East, and the latter will know enough to remain firm in the faith they have put in Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the last thirty years, notwithstanding the vituperations of the hon. Postmaster General.
I have carefully gone through the reports, and I have followed the whole debate in this connection since the opening of this session; we are not making of this a-party question for the city and harbour of Quebec, but we consider it a matter of the deepest concern for Canada as a whole. The hon. Postmaster General pretends to find a justification of the course followed in the restricted area available on Cape Diamond for the Transcontinental terminals. What does his knowledge of engineering amount to? I prefer the opinion of three noted engineers to his. In 1906, the Citizens' Committee of Quebec, comprising delegates of the city council and of the board of trade, and a representative of each of the railway and steamship companies, and of the shipping interests of Quebec, Montreal, the whole of Canada and even Great Britain, appointed Messrs. Ho are, Boswell and Doucet to prepare a report as to the most convenient site for the Transcontinental terminals. These three gentlemen submitted their conclusions in writing to that committee, and recommended building on the site of Champlain market and Cape Diamond the Transcontinental terminals, stations, deep water wharfs, sheds, shunting yards, local repair workshops, and these plans have been unanimously endorsed by the Citizens' Committee. All the railway companies on the south shore of the St. Lawrence in the district of Quebec, would have had the privilege of using such terminals after the bridge was built, and it was considered of enormous advantage to be able to build the stations, wharfs, etc., close to deep water. And now the hon. Postmaster General is endeavouring to give to this House the impression that all those people were astray as regards the sufficiency of space.
It is contended that union stations are rather the general rule nowadays; but it should not be forgotten that Quebec occupies a somewhat unique position to-day. It is a seaport, and we were intent on ensuring to the traffic during summer the immense advantage of direct transhipment from the cars to the ship, which would have materially cut down the general cost of transportation. Deep water wharfs
might have been constructed there at low cost over a distance of several miles, along which steamers of the highest tonnage might have loaded or unloaded at any time. Such were the main reasons which prompted the findings and recommendations of the engineers. The union station at the Palais is and will be especially of use to the Canadian Pacific railway which has at. that place no accommodation whatever for freight, and which will receive from the Government yearly interest on the cost of the station and a high rental as compensation for its use. Such is the embarrassment of the Government when it comes to give a plausible reason justifying the change in the plans, that the best they thought they could do was to unload the responsibility on one of their officials, Major Leonard. They even succeeded in having the statement endorsed by public bodies in Quebec, but it is childish to entertain the hope that the people of Quebec will give credence to such an explanation. Major Leonard was an official of that Government and the latter was in a position to exact compliance with its orders. Is there in the whole record a single word of protest on behalf of the Government against Major Leonard as regards his attitude towards Quebec? Not one. And it is only quite recently that the Government made that discovery. But no one will take any stock in their contention. Major Leonard's unfriendly stand is only the counterpart of hostility ehown in higher situations as regards Quebec; and whatever the Government may say, they are alone responsible for the delays incurred within the last three years in the carrying on of the work connected with the Transcontinental terminals in Quebec, to the detriment of that undertaking as well as of the whole of Canada.
For several months past the Transcontinental line has been practically open to circulation of trains; we were informed four or five days ago in this House that it would, be wholly completed by the month of 'September. However no provision whatever has. as yet been made in Quebec to meet the requirements of traffic. That unfortunate state of things is due wholly to the remissness of this Government. Within the last; three years not a single shovelful of eartha has been moved, not a single stone has been laid for the foundations of the necessary buildings which should by this time be completed.
The Liberal Government, it must be averred, had provided a series of magnifi-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in answer to some criti-12 m. cisms that have been made as to the course of the Government, in connection with the National Transcontinental railway. Nearly everything put forward by my hon. friends on the other side has been repeated two or three times before; but, as the charge is once more made, tfie answer must be once more given. It can perhaps be given in an even more effective way to-night than on previous occasions.
The first two paragraphs of my hon. friend's amendment which set forth the particulars of the default of the Government, refer to the alleged reduction in the standard of construction and to the absence of consent by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The hon. gentleman, if he had looked at the agreement of 1903 would not perhaps have fallen into the error into which apparently he has. Every hon. gentleman, including the mover of this resolution, who has spoken on the other side of the House, has obviously endeavoured to build up a case for the Grand Trunk Pacific against the country. They have taken it for granted that there has been some default on the part of the country, that the consent of the Grand Trunk has not been given to matters an respect of which its consent was required. If they had thought for one moment they would have known that their own law

officers, as far back as 1906, declared that the consent of the Grand Trunk is not required with respect to such matters. The then Minister of Justice and the Deputy Minister of Justice so advised them, and did so by reason of this provision contained in the fifth clause of the agreement made in 1903 between the Government and the company:
The said eastern division shall be constructed by and at the expense of the Government upon such a looation and according to such plans and specifications as it shall determine, having due regard to directness, easy gradients, and favourable curves.
The opinion of the law officers of the Crown in 1906 was that under this provision the location which includes gradients and curves, w'as entirely within the discretion of the Government, and that the discretion conferred upon the Government under clause 5 was not in the least reduced or removed by clause 7, which apparently is relied on by hon. gentlemen opposite.
But, putting aside for a moment the favourable position of the Government, which hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to break down against the interest of tne country, under the contract, w>nat does all this amount to? Upon whose advice has it been done? Is it to be expected that members of the Government-the Minister of Railways and the Postmaster General-snan follow the construction of this railway ana see that this curve or that or the other is of a proper proportion and that this grade or the other does not exceed a certain percentage? These hon. gentlemen know that they placed the construction of the eastern division of the National Transcontinental railway under a commission. They did that for a certain purpose, in order that it might be put into capable hands, that there might be, I suppose, no political interference, and that the work might be carried on in the best interests of the country. When we came into power we placed that work under the Charge of one of the most capable railway men we could find in Canada; but, more than that, we left the engineering part of it absolutely under the control of the very gentleman whom they themselves had selected, a gentleman of great eminence in his profession. Mr. Gordon Grant; and I tell them now that when they decry these gradients, when they endeavour to besmirch the very railroad which they themselves undertook to construct, they are casting reflections, not upon the Government, but upon the very engineer whom they selected as a man capable of carrying out this work. In order that there Should be

no mistake about that, I shall place upon ' Hansard ' a letter which I think has never yet been read, and which perhaps will give these gentlemen some light on the reasons and considerations which led to what they cail, without any foundation whatever, the degradation of this road. This letter was written by Mr. Gordon Grant on the 3rd of December, 1912, to the Minister of Railways and Canals, and is in these terms:
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Cochrane:
In accordance with your verbal request for an expression of my opinion as to the use of velocity grades on this, or any other line, and with special regard to the recent use of velocity grades on district ' C.'
l may say, that, disregarding ordinary sags in long fills, or fills over soft ground, that it has been considered inadvisable to bring up to profile grade at present and pay contractors' prices for this unnecesary work; there are, as you will see, only two cases that virtual grades have been adopted, and the saving effected by this slight change amount to $27,797.
They are both well within velocity limits and will not affect the hauling capacity of a locomotive to the extent of a single pound.
The introduction of virtual grades in railway construction for the purpose of economy in first cost and subsequent economy in operation by reason of reduced interest charges, cannot he considered other than a good business proposition.
In so far as this concerns the Transcontinental railway, I always was, and am still of opinion that virtual grades should have been used whenever it was practical and economical to do so, and that a very much larger amount of money could have been saved by their use, as the standard of grade adopted, together with the general topography of the country traversed by this line, effect a combination in favour of a virtual grade that an engineer will rarely or ever meet with.
I may also add that, in so far as I am personally concerned in this matter, while I was employed on this line, as a locating engineer, I used, in my location, virtual grades wherever it was practical, economical and common sense to do so.
I leave you to judge of my surprise when orders came from Ottawa that these grades would not he allowed, and that the profiles so made must be changed. This was accordingly done, which greatly increased the cost of construction, without, in any way, benefiting the line as regards operation.
Had these grades been adopted, where conditions warranted, if they ever did, the sags so introduced could have been removed wholly or in part by the operating company, at one-half the cost of contractors' prices, and the same applies to the permanent structures that would have been, in such cases, left out until more economical conditions obtained for their construction.
Tours truly,
Gordon Grant, Chief Engineer.

So that these hon. gentlemen, in attacking the Government for the course which has been taken by the commissioner of the Transcontinental railway, are in reality, attacking the very engineer whom they themselves appointed, and not attacking the Government at all, because every hon. gentleman in this House knows that in matters requiring the advantage of expert service, such as the construction of a railway, it would be most absurd foolishness on the part of any member of the Government who had not that expert knowledge to set himself up against an engineer eminent in his profession. This is their complaint', that we have followed for the purpose of economy, and for' the purpose of reduced cost of operation, the advice of the very engineer whom they themselves appointed, and have carried out the ideas which he said were based upon economy, common sense and the best practice of the engineering profession. This is what the tremendous speech of my hon. friend from St. John amounts to. He ventures to set up an opinion in a matter in which he is most profoundly ignorant, against that of a man at least as able as himself who has devoted his life to the study of problems such as this.

I have the opinion of
the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have the opinion of
the chief engineer of the Transcontinental railway appointed by the Government of which my hon. friend was' a member. Would the hon. gentleman have us believe that in respect of the construction of the Transcontinental railway, he and his Government were to take the advice not of the engineer whom they selected as best fitted for the purpose, but the advice of the engineer of the company whose interests might be profoundly different from those of this country in that regard? Does my hon. friend eay that it was the practice of the late Administration to reject the advice of their own engineer and accept the advice of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company? .

What I said was that
under the agreement of 1903 the plans and specifications were subject to the approval of the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have just alluded to
the advice of the law officers of the Crown,
who declared as far back as 1906 that the provisions of section 7 to which my hon. friends alluded did not in the least take away from the right of the Government under section 5 of the agreement to be guided by the judgment and opinion of their own engineers in respect of location, in respect of gradients, and in respect of curves. Therefore, when my hon. friend suggests that the Government should accept the advice of the Grand Trunk Pacific engineer instead of the advice of their own engineer, he is suggesting to the House that they should .accept that advice in respect of a matter which the Government was to judge and which the Grand. Trunk Pacific Railway Company was not to judge; and I leave it to the judgment of any hon. member of this House or of any man in this country as to whether or not that would have been a vise and justifiable proceeding on the part of the late Government or on the part of this Government. As a matter of fact what the commissioners of the Transcontinental railway did under the advice of their own engineer was this: they did precisely what the Grand Trunk Pacific has been doing In respect to the western division. They were leaving some work to be carried out after the road was put in operation because it could then be carriedoutatlesscost. And I want to tell my hon. friend, if he does not know it, that the Grand Trunk Pacific has been operating for four and a half years the lines in the prairie provinces. I have the certificate of the Government inspecting engineer, Mr. Schreiber, that that road is not completed to-day-that there is work still to be done on it. Why was that? Because the Grand Trunk Pacific knew in respect of that western division what the commissioners of the Transcontinental realized in respect of the eastern division, namely, that there was a good deal of work of that kind that could be done more economically after the road was in operation, and therefore, they left it to be done at that time; and if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company raise any question with regard to that, we can point to their own example and their own practice in respect to the western division. We can also justfy our course by the advice of the engineer of the Transcontinental railway appointed by the Government of which my hon. friends opposite were members at the time.
My right hon. friend the leader of the

Opposition has repeated a great many of his laments about the terminals at Quebec. He has not said anything new, but has repeated in another form what he has already said three or four times during the present session. He has alluded to the speech I made in Quebec last autumn. I am prepared to stand and do stand to-day by every word and every line of that speech, which was regarded as satisfactory, so far as I could learn, by the people of Quebec to whom it was addressed. I have it here under my hand, and I challenge my right hon. friend to point to one word or one line that has not been justified by subsequent events. He has stated here before Parliament that what he accomplished from 1903 to 1911 was to buy a piece of land at Cap Eouge, and he cannot point to anything else that he did, so far as I am aware. What have we done? I shall tell my right hon. friend what we have done in the three years as compared with what he and his party did during the eight years. In the first place, we have made arrangements to provide a ferry boat of large dimensions capable of holding a whole passenger train at one crossing. That boat was contracted for last year in Great Britain and I understand it will be delivered during the present season. It is to be used pending the completion of the Quebec bridge. We have provided ferry landings for that boat, and they were under construction last year when I spoke at Quebec. I do not know whether they have yet been completed, but I have no doubt that all due diligence is being exercised in their construction.
It is perfectly true that we have changed the location of the shops, which originally were to have been constructed at St. Foye. We propose to erect them at St. Malo, in the city of Quebec, and they are now in course of erection there. I am bound to say that during my visit to Quebec last autumn I did not find a single man who was willing to offer any criticism with regard to the change. The shops will occupy an area of about 200 acres, and a very large number of men will be employed. My right hon. friend knows it will be easier to secure the necessary labour in the city of Quebec than it would have been at St. Foye. Further, the site originally selected at St. Foye will not be useless. On the contrary, it will be utilized for a large through freight yard which is necessary at that point in order to provide for the distribution of cars on different roads.
We have already erected, as I mentioned lin my speech, a large handsome station at St. Foye, as well as an eighteen stall engine house and every building	necessary . for	the	efficient
operation of the railway. Between the Quebec bridge and the Champlain station a double track has been completed, and then there is a connection, which was alluded to only a day or two ago, with the Canadian Northern at Cap Eouge which permits entrance to the St. Charles side of the city, and which can be utilized for that purpose pending the completion of the tunnel that will connect the St. Lawrence water front with the new union station on the Palais site. I understood my right hon. friend to say that he intended to have a union station at the Champlain market, but he afterwards said that we had misunderstood him in that regard. I do not know that it would have been practicable to have a union station at the Champlain market.

What would
be the difference?
By means of a tunnel?
If you have a tunnel to connect between the St. Lawrence and the St. Charles, it is just as easy to have a tunnel to connect between the St. Charles and the St. Lawrence.

I did not understand that my right hon. friend contemplated a tunnel.
Sir WILFEID LAUEIEE. The railways were satisfied with the arrangement that was made.

Then, it was not to be
a union station?
I did not say it was a union station.

I understand my right
hon. friend to say now that a union station was not contemplated toy his Administration?
All the railways were satisfied.

Let us assume that all
the railways were satisfied, but was or was not a union station contemplated by the late Administration?
How are they going to get to Champlain market?

By the Quebec bridge.

Mir. .BORDEN: The Quebec bridge -would not be of much use for that purpose unless you moved it nine miles down the river.
Every railway coming to Quebec except the Canadian Pacific railway would come by way of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend has not made it very clear whether or not the late Administration contemplated a union station? I think that a union station at the Champlain market would not be practicable without a tunnel, and my right hon. friend wall not say that he did contemplate a tunnel. Therefore, I assume that it was not a union station that he contemplated, although he is reticent now as to whether he did have that in mind or not. While the tunnel that we propose is essential to the National Transcontinental for effective access to the union station on the St. Lawrence side of the river, I am informed by the commissioners that that tunnel will be equally necessary in the future to other railways in order that they may get access to the St. Lawrence water front. Therefore, it is not a question solely of the access of the Transcontinental railway to the Palais station and the St. Charles river side but it is also a question of the access of other railways to the St. Lawrence.
Only the Canadian Pacific railway.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well the Canadian Paci-fis railway is a fairly large railway.
The Canadian Northern railway as well.
No, the Canadian Northern will have access at St. Foye.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think that some time
ago my right hon. friend contended that the shops were not on the main line of railway.
Certainly not, but the Transcontinental railway is connecting with the Canadian Northern railway at St. Foye.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It will have access by
this short line of railway, the shops are on that line and if my right hon. friend relies on one side of the argument he must take the other side as well.

Does my right hon. friend believe that the location of the shops nine -miles from the main line, to -be connected by a spur line, will be equal to
shops on the main line? It does not matter if you have shops somewhere but certainly the working of the railway is improved by having the shops at St. Malo.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
These shops will have all the necessary connection with the main line of railway because pending the construction and completion of the tunnel there will he very good access to these shops, the St. Charles river front and the Palais station by means of the line which we have just acquired. I told the people of Quebec that:
Between the Quebec bridge and the Champlain market a double track has practically-been completed. There is also a connection with the Canadian Northern railway to Cap Rouge which permits entrance to the St. Charles side of the city, and which can be utilized for this purpose pending the completion of the tunnel that will connect the St. Lawrence water front with the new union station on the Palais site. While that tunnel is essential to the National Transcontinental railway for effective access to the union station and to the St. Charles side, it will be equally necessary to other great railway systems which will naturally acquire access to the great frontage terminals on the St. Lawrence.
I believe this is a good -common sense view of the situation; at all events, it was one which was communicated to me by the commissioner of the Transcontinental railway, -and I had very good reasons to rely on it. Then, I understand it is good practice in railway construction- and in providing terminals to have, if possible, one union station for all the railway systems entering the city. So it was decided that this great railway station should be erected on the Palais site. What I said about it at that time I say now, that it will be a very handsome edifice worthy Doth of the city and of the great railways by which it is to be used. Not only will this building be handsome and spacious, but its arrangement and accommodation will be of the most modern and approved design. Its location is in the most populous part of the city, and it will therefore accommodate most conveniently the greatest number of people. Under these circumstances I do not see why the right hon. gentleman has bad dreams over the situation, and why he disturbs us so -at this stage of the session by repeating what he has said three or four times already.
Further than that, let us see what we have done at the city of Quebec, as compared with the wonderful activity of our predecessors that resulted in the acquisition of some land at St. Foye, and not much else as far as I can see. We have
51C4

acquired three miles of the best water front at Quebec, extending from Sillery to Cape Diamond, and portions of the water front from Cape Diamond to Champlain market have also been secured. What I said in Quebec at that time I stand by to-day. These are my words:
The magnificent waterfront will give to the Government and to the Harbour Commission the opportunity of almost unlimited development of port and terminal facilities; and I hope you will agree that In thus looking forward to the possibilities of the future the Government have taken no unwise course. In adopting this policy we feel that we are acting not in the interest of Quebec alone but in the interest of all Canada, for Canada as a whole is concerned in the provision of modern and effective facilities necessary for the outflow and inflow of commerce at all its great ports.
Further than that, I pointed out that whenever necessary we could arrange for connection from the Champlain market station to Louise Basin for the transfer of freight, which can largely be carried on at night without disturbance or inconvenience to the business activities of the city.
In addition to that, my right hon. friend will perhaps like to be reminded that whereas he absolutely forgot, in so far as we are aware, the necessities of the great city and port of Quebec in respect to dry dock facilities, we are building to-day opposite Quebec one of the greatest dry docks in the world, which dry dock is absolutely necessary for the commerce which will in the early future flow in ever-increasing volume to the city and port of Quebec. My right hon. friend says we have not done anything, and yet we have done that. As compared with his mighty efforts which resulted in the acquisition of a couple of hundred acres of land at St. Foye, we have accomplished these things; and yet my right hon. friend has the courage to stand up and criticize this Government that has done five times more in three years than he accomplished during the eight years that this transcontinental railway was under construction.
There are a great many other things of which I would like to remind my right hon. friend. We reconstituted the harbour commission in the city of Quebec, and what have they done since that time as compared with what was done during the regime of my right hon. friend? Let me point out to him that they drew, up a general scheme for the future, as well as the immediate, development of the harbour. They called together all those interested in the harbour, tne business interests, the officials of

the railway companies, the steamship lines, the pilots and all other persons who could throw any light upon the best method of development; and they took counsel with them. Having done that, they caused plans to be prepared by competent engineers, and in accordance with these plans, contracts have been let. Some of the works are completed and some are now under construction. The bulkhead wall on the St. Charles side is in course of construction and dredging contracts involving no less than 3,000.000,000 cubic yards have been awarded for dredging at the mouth of the St. Charles. A contract has also been given to capable contractors for the construction of an elevator having a capacity of 1,000,000 bushels with the possibility of arrangements being made for increasing the capacity to 2,500,000 bushels with very little -outlay. I understand that the elevator itself has already been completed.
Completed and ready.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yet, my right hon friend, whose eight years of activity resulted in the acquisition of a couple of hundred acres of land, has seen fit to- jibe at us with this splendid record of what we have actually accomplished staring him in the face all the time. I cannot understand the condition of mind that has led my right hon. friend to take that position. In addition to that I would like to- tell him, if he is entirely oblivious of the fact, that freight sheds have been constructed for the Grand Trunk and Intercolonial and new tracks laid in connection with the -car ferry. I went all over these works when I was last at Quebec, and I was astonished at the progress which had been made in extending the facilities which had been provided there. Besides the things which I have enumerated, shunting engines have been purchased and are now being used with good results in increased efficiency. Indian Cove has been acquired by the commission, a small mill has been erected for the purpose otf working up the timber foT the cribs and a number of large cribs have been constructed there for the purpose of the work which is toeing carried on in the St. Charles river. My right hon. friend should go to Quebec at some convenient time and look at those works; and if he does he will come back with an inspiration which will not cause him to stand up and find fault with the Government for having succeeded so admirably with works that stood still during the eight years from 1903 to 1911.

But that is not all. The Government acquired a portion of the water front of the St. Lawrence, three miles in extent, to which I have already alluded. This naturally caused some difficulty on the part of persons who had been utilizing that water front, and it was thought necessary to make some provision on the front of the St. Charles river. What did we do in that regard? We did not sit down and fold our arms, as the late Administration did. We thought it important and desirable that provision should be made for the improvement of the St. Charles above the railway bridge, near the Louise Basin. The construction of a dam and other works at that point would enable some six miles of the St. Charles river to be used for transportation, and we have been dealing with the work there. I think the contract had been given for the lock when I was in Quebec.
Yes, we had given that contract.
When was that water front acquired?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Which water front?
The water front that my right hon. friend speaks of. Was it not acquired by the commission under Mr. Parent?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There was a right of way acquired, but as I understand it, the water front was not.
I think it was.

You are mistaken
about that; it was bought under Major Leonard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The right of way was acquired under the late Government, but the water front was not.
That is right.

Mr. Parent spoke to me as Minister of Public Works about it, and I advised him to acquire the water front as well, because I thought it would be done more cheaply, and I am under the impression he did so.
No, he did not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) will find in regard to that as in regard to a great many other matters in Quebec under the late Government that it all ended in talk, and when we came into power we found it necessary to acquire the
water front which hon. gentlemen opposite had not acquired. When I was in Quebec I had the honour of being present at the commencement of the work on the St. Charles lock. The contracts had been let and the work is being carried on by a competent contractor.
Under all these circumstances I think that the record of the present Administration in respect to the terminals at Quebec compares most favourably with the record of the late Liberal Government. Indeed, I hardly like to put it that way; I would rather say that looking at what was not done by the Liberal Government in the eight years from 1903 to 1911, and looking at what has been done by this Government in the two and a half years since it has come into power, there is absolutely no comparison between the records of the two. In the one case there was nothing done by the Liberal Government during eight years, while in the other case there has been accomplished in two and a half years by the Conservative Government more than they did in the whole eight years; nay, more than they accomplished in the whole fifteen years of their administration, so far as the development of the harbour of Quebec is concerned.
Let me allude for a moment to the complaint of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) with regard to the operation of the Transcontinental railway in New Brunswick. The hon. gentleman seems to be continually under the delusion that the Government have the right undeT the contract of 1903 to force the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to operate a portion of the line. I say to him that the Government have not the right to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate a portion of the line. The Government can negotiate with them, but they cannot compel them.
That is all I said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then, what fault has the hon. gentleman to find?
That you have not tried to negotiate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We did negotiate with
them. We negotiated with them in New Brunswick and elsewhere, and the net result was that when we found ourselves unable to conclude with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in respect to the operation of the line in New Brunswick, an arrangement which we thought in the interests of the country, we undertook the operation of that line by the Intercolonial railway.

and that portion of it which is not still under construction is to-day being operated by the Intercolonial railway. In these circumstances I believe that the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) will justly fall upon deaf ears in this House.
Hear, hear.

But not outside the
House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That remains to be seen. My hon. friend (Mr. Gauvreau) poses very frequently as a prophet, but we shall see later to what extent his assumption of that role is justified. I can only reiterate once more that we have done infinitely more for the development of the harbour of Quebec in less than three years than did the Liberal Government in all the fifteen years during which they held office, and it ill becomes them to criticise this Government in view of the splendid work it is carrying on there.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsley) negatived on division.
Main motion agreed to, <and the House went into Committee of Supply.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Borden, the House adjourned at 12.45 a.m., Tuesday.
Tuesday, June 9, 1914.
